utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We apologise for the lateness of the start, which is explained by the inclement weather conditions. Mr. Nice, we are to deal with the admission of documents as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, and I wonder if I could, on this occasion only, just take a couple of minutes to identify again the structural issues and perhaps difficulties that we face, because I think they're likely to recur, although they occurred with particular clarity in the case of this witness and perhaps are best revealed in the outstanding issue that there still is before the Chamber; how to deal with the extract from the article published in Nacional, being an interview with Dusan Bilandzic. The paradigm problem that we face, or issue that we face is this: The Prosecution presents its case, the Defence broadens it - absolutely no objection to that at all. So in the Bilandzic example, we presented evidence, direct evidence, of what actually happened at the meeting between the accused and Tudjman. The defendant broadens it by seeing what was said in the meetings that followed that meeting. There are meetings between the working party, first through Smilja Avramov - we did not accept her account at all - and then through the last witness, and we didn't accept that at all. We then, in the broadened case, offer material that would support our position, the position we do take on the broader issue. In this case it's the newspaper interview, and the issue, I suppose, for the Judges -- for the Court is this: Should the document be admitted; and if so, would one of the following four things perhaps happen: One, in the absence of any more evidence, could the Tribunal, because of there being no rule against hearsay, act on the article of Bilandzic and make a finding contrary to the evidence of the two live witnesses? Well, theoretically possible but inconceivable. The second possibility: If other evidence emerged in line with what is said by Bilandzic in the article, it's either in evidence or possibly if evidence from which very strong inference is consistent with what's in the newspaper article arise, might the Chamber rely on the newspaper article, saying, "Well, we make this conclusion and observe that there is material consistent with it from elsewhere." Possible, it would seem to me. Third possibility is that the Prosecution would, at the rebuttal stage - and notwithstanding what His Honour Judge Kwon said about the possibility of a more generous approach to rebuttal, the Prosecution has in mind that in general in these courts rebuttal cases are concise and there are reasons why it would be wanted to be in this case - the Prosecution might seek to call Bilandzic, for example. And then the fourth possibility that is having the exhibit as an exhibit, the Chamber is in a position, if it decides that it wants to consider calling any witnesses itself, to assess whether this witness or this potential witness is one to call. And that sort of issue arises particularly where the case is broadened by the accused in the way that he has quite properly done. I have no objection to that. On the contrary. And I suppose metaphorically, it's having an exhibit and it's being on the shelf. Just to go into the history for two minutes: 92 bis was generated, I think, by a decision of this Chamber in respect of the signed witness statement of a witness who was dead at the time, as Your Honour will recall. I think His Honour Judge Robinson will recall. And the admission of the statement by this Chamber, as then composed, was overruled by the Appeals Chamber, and very greatly, though I respected the composition of that particular Appeals Chamber, I always regretted that I wasn't able to argue because the matter was dealt with on paper, that it seemed to me that the admission of the document by the Chamber presided over by the late Sir Richard May was really on the basis of we need this document now because other material may come in for which we will assess it, and that was really the way I had understood the ruling of the Court, as it were, putting it on the shelf and having it available. And it may be that the Court will think that that approach is consistent with or more consistent with the approach of a civil system Bench having material that's important to it for consideration in its truth-finding function, given that it is a truth-finding Court and not a proof-resolving Court. Proof there has to be but within the broader function of truth. So, Your Honours, that's our approach, and we would invite you, with perhaps those observations in mind, to take a fairly generous approach to the admission of exhibits, recognising that they can metaphorically be put on the shelf for later determination. The documents that have been produced, if I can list them, as I understand the position by us are, first of all, Exhibit 816, which is an exhibit. That's the article by the witness. Second, the extract from Smilja Avramov's book, which was exhibited as 817. Then there was Exhibit 818, marked for identification, which was the book Kosovo -- or the extract from the book Kosovo: Law and Politics, Kosovo in Normative Acts Before and After 1974, and I would ask the Chamber to admit that document. The Chamber will recall, as I explained at the beginning, that the various laws that we looked at within that are hard to find elsewhere and we haven't found them all elsewhere. In the expanded case of the accused, those laws, following on the 89 amendments may be of considerable significance showing what happened to Kosovo Albanians in circumstances where the accused, through his witnesses, now really asserts that the Albanians were victims of nothing and bringers of everything upon themselves. As I explained right at the beginning, that Exhibit 818 contains some commentary but I haven't taken you to the commentary. Indeed, insofar as I adopt the commentary I have tried to adopt it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please correct me if I'm wrong: All parts dealt with in that by you say enactments or laws in relation to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No other parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No other parts, no. And I don't desire -- yes. Ms. Dicklich reminds me, in fact, you have the entire book. It's a rather slender book, published by what we would hope would be characterised as an independent organisation, but Your Honour is quite right, it's laws that we've referred to, or extracts from laws. So there it is. The next document was Exhibit 819 that I've already referred to, the article from Nacional that the Chamber has yet to decide upon, and I'm not pressing it to decide today. Exhibit 820 was the article about Seselj's qualifications for professorship, and that's been exhibited as the video clip 821 and 821.1. Then 822 is the article by Kelmendi marked for identification, and the Court will remember that this document gave an account of a history of an application to overturn the 1989 constitutional amendments. I explained to Your Honours that it was difficult to find these documents that are referred to in this proposed exhibit, and I'm holding it up just to remind you what it looks like. The good news is that we have, through repeated efforts, located at the moment only in B/C/S the application and the judgement of the Constitutional Court of Kosovo, and you may remember that in the article, the judgements are numbered 54/90 of the 27th of July of 1990, and the documents that we have, I think, bear those -- bear those numbers. So what I would ask the Chamber to do in respect of that exhibit is to allow the -- allow the exhibit to be produced. I'm told the English translations will be available tomorrow, and I'd ask that the actual application and the judgement of the Constitutional Court could be associated with that exhibit, perhaps as -- well, whatever the number is, parts A and B, something to that effect. The next exhibit would be the document that corrects and completes the Defence Exhibit tab 47. The Chamber will recall that the witness yesterday accepted that he had intentionally cut down tab 47 of his own to cut off from the end of it references to the international presence and human rights, and it was quite wrong that that should have happened, in our submission, and we have a document published as part of The Crisis in Kosovo 1989 to 1999, and if that complete version of tab 47 could go in as a Prosecution Exhibit, we'd be grateful. And then the next -- the only other two potential documents that I'd ask the Chamber to give consideration to are documents that are built on my earlier -- my opening observations, which I won't have to repeat again in the trial. The Chamber will remember that at a time when time was very short with this witness, I said to him that he'd been subject to heavy criticism by a lawyer from his own university in an article on the constitution headed the Unbearable Lightness of Constitutional Being, or Unconstitutional Being, and separately that he's been heavily criticised in public for his latest book, his latest constitutional law book. And the question for the Chamber, if I may say so, is this: Where a witness of this kind, although nominally a fact witness clearly a witness whose expertise underpins or is really what he's giving evidence about, where he's presented in the way he was by this accused - as it were, the unimpeachable authority - it is important that the Court should know of material to a contrary effect. Now, I haven't actually dealt with the -- with all the exhibits because there are some more that have been produced, including the ones where -- the one from Slobodan Samardzic, which I must perhaps also turn to, but I would invite the Chamber to consider, again addressing itself on the basis that it is not unlike a civil system of Court, I would invite the Chamber to consider whether it shouldn't have or have available to it publicly broadcast criticisms by other academics of both the constitutional position - I think The Unbearable Lightness of Constitutional Being includes the reference to the constitution being drafted in only five days, something that the witness dealt with in evidence in a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, why do you say that the system here is more akin to a truth-finding, proof-resolving --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because under the Rules and in determining how evidence is to be given, the Rules make it clear - I'll have the Rule to hand in a second - that it's with a view to establishing the truth. It sets out the word "truth" in the Rules as opposed to just proof, which is what, unspoken, underlies the ordinary adversarial process. The Rule sets out specifically that the adduction of evidence is with a view to establishing the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And on that basis alone you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I think that that basis is sufficient. Of course, the truth-finding function, as identified in the Rules for the Court in no way, in no way changes the burden on the Prosecution on all the evidence of establishing proof beyond reasonable doubt, of course. But given that the argument of a prosecution is based on all the evidence ultimately before the Trial Chamber, and given that the Trial Chamber's duty under the Rules is so to deal with evidence in a way as to establish the truth, I respectfully suggest my argument on how material should be assembled is an appropriate one, namely that it should be assembled or accepted by the Chamber with a view to this truth-finding function at the end of the exercise. The alternative, if the issue is thrown entirely back to the Prosecution, is that on issues like this, there would have to be a very formalistic item-by-item application for evidence in rebuttal and I would invite you to say that that's not desirable in the broader way these cases have to be dealt with. So I invite the Chamber - obviously it hasn't had a chance to read it now and I wouldn't ask it to do so now - to look at the two public criticisms of the witness by Stefan Lilic from his own university, different department but the same legal faculty, I think, with a view to deciding whether that material in cross-examination that was inevitably cut short not least because of the way the witness -- not cut short but wasn't able to cover everything because of the way -- not least because of the way the witness answered questions, I'd asked you to consider in due course having those. And then, of course, there's the other articles we looked at yesterday. There's Exhibit 823, the article dealing with whether the accused had a right to a third term. That's already been exhibited. The Article 824 that has already been exhibited, and then there was the critical article that we looked at in part but that everybody had opportunity to read over several days by Slobodan Samardzic, and I'd invite the Chamber to make that available as an exhibit. Your Honours, I don't know if I can help any further with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, thank you very much. Let us hear from Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a couple of general observations in response to Mr. Nice and then I wish to take you very briefly through my observations and objections to the MFI documents which have been referred to. Firstly, in relation to the general comments and observations by Mr. Nice, he refers to a broadening of the case by the accused. It might be better referred to and bracketed as an exploration of the case, which is of course a perfectly legitimate exercise by an accused, and in my submission, the most appropriate route for Mr. Nice in dealing with his evidence is the route which is already provided for in Rule 85(A)(iii), which is of course the rebuttal stage of evidence, it being, of course, a matter of judgement for the Prosecutor as to how wide and which issues he chooses to deal with in rebuttal. Leaving those general observations aside and if I may now move briefly on to the MFI documents. The first one, which is MFI 818, Kosovo: Law and Politics, briefly my observations are these: As Your Honour Judge Kwon has rightly observed, it is a collection of laws and decisions, constitutional laws and decisions which were drawn to the attention of the witness and commented on by him. They have not been exhibited to date. They are general constitutional documents, and one point of view may be to raise the question as to why they hadn't been produced, as arguably they may have been during that case. Of further concern is the political comment which was referred to by Mr. Nice, which is found at page 9 of the document. Those are my observations. And of course, if Your Honours were minded to admit the document, I would ask and submit that only those documents which were referred to should be admitted, and I do have the page references for Your Honours if that would assist. Moving on, if I may, to MFI 819, which was the Nacional newspaper article, Your Honours will recall that during the evidence of this witness, Ratko Markovic, it was not accepted by him the version that was produced in relation to the working group meetings that were held. His Honour Judge Robinson raised the question of the status of the newspaper report earlier on, I think it was last week, which hadn't in fact been confirmed by this witness, and that was followed by comments and observations and concerns by His Honour Judge Bonomy, questioning the timing of the presentation of this evidence during the Defence phase and the fact that the document had not been accepted by the witness. Your Honours may also recall that in relation to this Nacional newspaper article, the Prosecution conceded last week that it may be able to deal with the views of this witness in other ways. Of course, the issues of provenance and reliability are also important for the Trial Chamber to consider. Mr. Nice has referred to it being important that the Trial Chamber has this information before it. In my submission, it already does. It has heard the observations, the extracts commented, and those comments by the witness in response, and there is no need or in fact no basis for this article to be made an exhibit in the case. Dealing briefly with two other matters: MFI 822, which is the Kelmendi article, in fact it's produced -- a document produced by the Kosovar Information Centre and it's the Discriminatory and Unconstitutional Act document. Mr. Nice asked several questions on this document and asked the witness to confirm what was contained within it was factually correct. The witness dealt with that, and his answers, as Your Honours may recall, were to the first question, "I don't know"; to the second, he didn't agree. He didn't adopt anything in the document. Again, it's an article by someone else who is not a witness in the case. It was not produced through the Prosecution case, and in any event, I would ask Your Honours to be beware of the political comment contained in the foreword, even if you were minded to accept it contrary to my observations. The last document I wish to refer briefly to is the article referred to by Mr. Nice which has not been given an MFI number, and that's the article by Slobodan Samardzic. Again, the concerns are these: Firstly, document written by somebody who is not a witness in the case and is not available to be cross-examined on views contained therein by the accused or anyone else. Secondly, it's not a Prosecution Exhibit presented in the case to date, and I raise the same concern: It is a document of general nature on general constitution system of the FRY, and again it's arguable that it may have been able to be produced in their case. Mr. Nice read the passages to the witness, and in my submission, that is sufficient again. It's not necessary for this or any basis for this to become an exhibit in the case. As a concluding remark, Your Honours, the references by Mr. Nice to the truth and the finding of truth, the difficulties which Your Honours will be aware of are these: When the admission of evidence is on the basis of an inquisitorial system or approach to the admission of evidence, the presentation of evidence in this courtroom is still governed by an accusatorial approach where the parties are under an obligation to challenge evidence which is not accepted and therefore the admission of reams of evidence into the case presents an onerous obligation on the accused to confront and deal with that evidence which has and should have been produced under the general principle that a Prosecution should produce its evidence during its phase of the case, there being provision for rebuttal at the end if further presentation is required. Your Honours, those are my observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, what would you say to the admission of a perfect version of Contact Group decision, and Mr. Nice also referred to a Constitutional Court decision referred to by -- in relation to the recent amendment of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, in relation to the first document Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that you've raised, which has been produced in part, I have no observations to make on that. Your Honour may direct his comments to Mr. Milosevic. I have no -- no observations to make on that point, it may be that he does. The second issue, in fact, relates to an article which I've taken issue with. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's 822.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's right, the Kelmendi article. So on the basis of my submissions, I would ask that none of that go in. If Your Honours are minded to put in the article, then to make sense of it Your Honours may require to have those documents to hand, but my concern is this: Those documents were not produced during the testimony of the witness, and the witness, who was a constitutional man of great knowledge, was not given the opportunity to deal with them. So I would urge the Trial Chamber to exercise caution in that regard even if you were minded to admit the Kelmendi article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Higgins. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Nice submitted a whole package of completely useless papers. You can decide what you wish about them in accordance with the previous practice, but I would like to lodge an objection. Mr. Nice speak about the so-called decision of the Constitutional Court of Kosovo. This decision of the Constitutional Court of Kosovo was never adopted. This is what we were told by the witness. What Mr. Nice produced is a draft decision that was prepared by the members of that Constitutional Court, just as there was a draft decision on declaring Kosovo a republic, and so on. Therefore, it has no value, no worth at all. However, if he continues to insist upon that, then, yes, we can discuss this piece of paper as a draft that has no legal value. That is completely clear based on what we heard here. As for the credibility of the witness, I believe that it is not proper to introduce into evidence this article which according to Mr. Nice sharply criticised the witness, and that that was done by Professor Lilic, also a university professor. You will remember that because of the lack of time, Mr. Nice did not even give an opportunity to the witness to respond to those criticisms. All he was able to say was a few words about the article of Professor Samardzic and point out that he was not a lawyer, but as for the article which sharply criticised the witness, he had no opportunity to respond to that at all, and therefore, it should be insignificant. Mr. Nice explained how somebody wrote the constitution in five days, and that's absurd. They're ignoring the fact that there was a working group consisting of constitutional experts from Montenegro and Serbia, and these people spent together a whole week shut in a room working on drafting the constitution. Mr. Nice completely ignored that all of these people had at least 15 years of prior experience in drafting these documents. Therefore, this kind of criticism as directed by Mr. Nice is completely pointless. Therefore, these documents gathered together by Mr. Nice have just one purpose; to add to the paperwork. Otherwise, they're completely worthless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I make a couple of points?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't want to prolong this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I know that, Your Honour, but just to say that the relevant Rule to which I referred to is 90(F) where the exercise and control "over the mode and order of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence" is to "make the interrogation and presentation effective for the ascertainment of the truth; and to avoid the needless consumption of time," and it would be my submission that both of those limbs support my general proposition. Other than that, I would simply draw to your attention -- so that's the provision I rely on. I'll go back to what I said as to presentation of evidence or assembly of materials for evidence, truth is indeed important as is the needless consumption of -- avoiding the needless consumption --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, (F)(i) is as applicable, in my view, to the common law adversarial system as it is to the civil law inquisitorial system. In the common law adversarial system we are also concerned with making the interrogation and presentation effective for the ascertainment of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may say so, defending advocates in a position to take technical arguments for the exclusion of evidence would not have to face a codified test of that kind in an adversarial system, and I have regularly been in a position to take the advantage of not having to face such a test. This is much more specific. Your Honours, one other thing that I ought to draw to your attention, and that is that outstanding in your consideration is whether, for example, you might wish to hear again from the constitutional expert who was called, Dr. Kristan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm going to make a ruling on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll just tell you now, but we will require you, within a week, to make a filing identifying the areas in respect of which you wish to adduce evidence from Dr. Kristan should you wish to recall him, and also to comment on his availability.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, I'm very grateful for that because I was going to say that you will have appreciated from the research that we've been able to make that there are indeed lawyers who may be in a position apparently to assist where lawyers have been unwilling, for the reasons given before, to come to this Court. We do not yet know, apart from Dr. Kristan, whether such witnesses may now be inclined and willing or whether their previous attitude will be reinforced, but it's helpful to know that we can have the opportunity of applying for Dr. Kristan and we'll deal with that immediately. I'm grateful for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In translation into Serbian, it was stated that the -- that the "defending counsel" who did not want to participate or didn't wish to come, whereas in English the word used was the "lawyers," and there's a great difference. "[In English]... Lawyers who may be in position apparently to assist where lawyers have been unwilling to..." [Interpretation] Therefore, "lawyer" and "Defence counsel" are two different things. "Defence counsel" has to be a lawyer, but in Serbian language, "advokat" or Defence counsel is somebody appearing in court, not just lawyer as a legal expert. So I would like to draw your attention to this and so that you can ensure that the translation is proper. And another matter that I omitted to mention: When explaining the exhibit which is actually an exhibit under tab 47 presented by myself, which are the principles of the Contact Group, Mr. Nice said that it was as though somebody covered up the fact that there was international participation in settling the Kosovo crisis. Therefore, please take a look at tab 47. You have texts both in English and in Serbian entitled General Elements. And the last among those elements - it has ten bullets - is: "International involvement and full cooperation by the parties concerning implementation." Therefore, this is contained in the principles given under tab 47. And as the witness stated, this was a delegation of the government of Serbia that accepted these principles as presented by the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll give a decision on the Prosecution potential exhibits later. And in relation to Defence exhibits, I am reminded that tabs 9 and 12 of Defence Exhibit 271 were actually referred to but not admitted, and so we will admit those; tabs 9 and 12 of D271. Mr. Milosevic, of course the time spent in this -- in discussing this matter does not count in respect of time allocated to you. You will now call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I call witness Mitar Balevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may commence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Balevic.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milosevic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us where you come from, where you were born, and where you lived for the longest part of your life.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Montenegro in 1929. From age 4 I went to live in Metohija with my parents in a village in Budisavci Municipality, Pec region, the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. Therefore, I spent the majority of my life in Kosovo and Metohija until the expulsion in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation? Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I am currently retired, a retired railroad worker, and I will read relevant bits of my working biography. In 1947 and up until 19 -- from 1947 to 1973, I worked in the railway company. In May 1997, due to -- in May 1987, due to pressure, I left the railroad company and went to work in Obud in Cetinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it in 1987 or did you make a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: It was in 1977. And in the month of May, I returned back to work as a railroad worker. In the meantime, for four years, I represented Yugoslav Rails in Bulgaria between 1979 and 1984. Upon my return from Bulgaria, I continued working in the railroad company as an advisor to the director of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, there is no need for you to make such long pauses.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I can't hear anything in my headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is nothing that you need to hear right now. As you are speaking, there is no interpretation going into your language.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Then for a while I was a secretary of the traffic community interest group, and then -- then I retired on the 4th of April, 1990. And starting in 1994, I volunteered within the Socialist Party of Serbia in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were also a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I became a member of the youth organisation in 1945, and then in 1949, I became a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also held some party posts, as we could see from your biography.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I held almost all party functions on a volunteer basis. I was a secretary member of the Regional Committee, member of -- or president of the regional conference and of the Municipal Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, in one stage of the developments in Kosovo in the 1980s, there was much talk about the self-organising of Serbs and Montenegrins in order to resist the pressure which they were under in order to move out, and it is well known that you were quite active in this process of self-organising. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Due to various pressure -- pressures exerted on Serbs and Montenegrins, I participated in this process of self-organising. I participated in various gatherings, meetings, all aimed at stopping this terror and allowing these people to remain living in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You lived that entire time in Pristina and Kosovo Polje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: From 1961 to 1980 I lived in Kosovo Polje. Then starting in 1980 until the 26th of July, when I was forced to leave the town, I lived in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of your experience and the posts you held in Pristina and Kosovo Polje, in view of all of your activities that we just mentioned, could we say that you are very well-informed about all of the events from that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell me, based on your knowledge -- therefore please focus on what you know, not on some historical facts. Therefore, when did Serbs start suffering from Albanian nationalism in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs and Montenegrins started suffering from that in 1941, based on my knowledge. That started during the occupation and the attack on Yugoslavia. Rather, that was during the Second World War. At the time, many Serbs and Montenegrins were forced to leave Kosovo and Metohija. Their houses were burned. They were expelled. There were even some murders. Therefore, that was the first form of pressure that I'm aware of and I can tell you about. Tens of thousands of Serbs and Montenegrins left Kosovo and Metohija at that time. Their houses and the entire property was burned. Real property was looted. Tens of thousands left Kosovo and Metohija. During the war, a large number of Albanians moved in, were relegated to the area. These figures could be verified, and according to what I know, 200.000 Albanians were relegated to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and they occupied the property vacated by Serbs and Montenegrins. At the time, the German forces were stationed in Kosovo and Metohija, in the northern part. The part that I lived in was occupied by Italian forces, who I have to say treated the local population decently, whereas the other part was held by Bulgarian forces. That was the military power. However, the civilian authorities were Albanian. This process continued after the war in 1945. Let me tell you that, according to the official facts and documents, Dzafer Deva, leader of Albanians from Kosovska Mitrovica, in a gathering, stated: "The freedom has come. Yugoslavia is no more. The Greater Albania has been created. Serbs ought to be expelled from the Balkans or killed." Between 1941 and 1944 is the period that I must say the following about: At the time, Boro and Ramiz were killed in 1944 in the process of this terror committed against Serbs. They were in a shelter in Djakovica. And when Svetozar Vukmanovic, Tempo, called them to go to Prizren --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, you don't need to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you this just to illustrate the terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we don't need to go into those details because very few people here know who Boro and Ramiz were. One was a Serb and the other one was an Albanian and they worked together, and this is another example of harmony that these people lived in. But tell us, what happened after World War II? What can you say about the events after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: The intensity of the Albanian nationalism gradually increased. One of the gravest moments immediately after the war was when the state leadership of Yugoslavia and its leaders adopted a law or a decision, I don't know what it was called, banning the return of Serbs and Montenegrins to Kosovo, those who had left Kosovo during the war. Whether consciously or unconsciously, the Albanians were assisted by the leaders of the Yugoslav state, and that was a terrible document to be enacted which banned the Serbs and Montenegrins to return to their homeland. That was one of the terrible moments. Another terrible event came in 1966 for us Serbs and Montenegrins, the communists, because the fourth plenary session was held, the infamous one, at which Rankovic was removed from office and expelled from the party. That was the crash of the security network for Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There was no translation for that. Would you try again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now hearing it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, I was saying, do you remember the demonstrations that took place in 1968?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I do, but I just wanted to raise one more question that I didn't do a moment ago, and that is what I wanted to say: For the Serbs and Montenegrins, it was a catastrophic constitution, the one enacted in 1974, when the provinces or, rather, the province of Kosovo was an autonomous province and Serbia was neither a state nor a province. In 1981 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you now, sir, is whether you have any recollections about the 1968 demonstrations. Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: They were the first demonstrations that were held, and the object of those demonstrations was the following: Kosovo Republic, first and foremost; and secondly, to be joined to Albania and secede from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what brought about this outflow of Albanian nationalism and separatism which escalated in the 1968 events and also in the events in 1981 that you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the basic aspirations of all those demonstrations was for Kosovo to secede, to break away from Serbia. And the only reason -- that was the only reason for the demonstrations. There was no other reason except that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me please, was that stated openly or was it something that was hidden?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: The demonstrations, especially the 1981 demonstrations that were designed to topple the system, came out with public demands calling for -- or, rather, when I'm talking -- mentioning the Albanians here, I'm not talking about all the Albanians, I'm talking about the terrorists, the people that did evil to the Serb people. But the demonstrations in 1988 with their brutality and force, which were later on stifled by intervention on the part of the army when the provisional leadership called it in, they demonstrated fully what kind of demands were being made; the demand for Kosovo Republic, for Kosovo to break away. And at that time, the Albanians had all their rights, they enjoyed full rights, and I will quote just come of those rights. They enjoyed the right to their own Assembly, to their own Executive Council, to their Presidency, to their own Supreme Court, to their own Constitutional Court, to their Ministry of the Interior, a large university, everything except an army, and they didn't need an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me this: I'm just asking you about your own firsthand knowledge and experience here. When did you hear about the term "an ethnically pure Kosovo"? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: "An ethnically pure Kosovo" was a term that was heard at the very beginning, but in 1950 -- in the 1950s, it gained particular expression. And this so-called -- or not so-called but actual ethnically pure Kosovo was started, and the Serbs and Montenegrins started to move out. In the second half of the 1960s, this took on a massive character and this was influenced by the demonstrations that took place in 1968. So for an ethnically pure Kosovo and of an ethnically pure Kosovo I learnt about at the beginning of the 1950s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what means at that time, and please bear in mind your own personal experience, what you yourself know, what method of pressure was exerted against the Serbs, exerted by the Albanian nationalists against the Serbs? What pressure did they exert?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the Albanians resorted to all types of exertion and means of exertion. They were just somewhat different from World War II. I'm sure they got support from abroad, but they applied all this pressure against the Serbs and Montenegrins. There was killing, rape, torching of property, confiscation of property, the usurpation of property, pilfering, plundering, looting, other forms of abuse and mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So they used all the means at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the means at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me please, do you know anything about what took place in the 1980s and 1990s, certain events during that period of time or, rather, personally were you aware of the torching of the patriarchy on the 16th of March, 1981?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am personally aware of that. I do know that parts of the lodges of the patriarchy were torched. I was on the spot many times, and it was also a question discussed at our party meetings, why this came about, because people were trying to supply erroneous information, that it was through intent that they were torched, and this was a sign to the Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was a sign and a call to them to move out. Do you remember the killing of Miodrag Saric and the Martinovic case, and Danilo Milincic and so on and so forth? Much was written about those individual cases of killing and abuse. Now I'm not asking about what you read about in the press but were you personally an eyewitness of those events took place in Kosovo at that period of time, so these several killings that gave rise to public consternation?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the case of Djordje Matinovic [phoen] is a case which was unprecedented before that and I'm sure will not happen again. Harm was done to him with a broken bottle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not go into detail.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But I am aware of that case and I happen to have been in the hospital for some other reason when people came to visit him. There was a Colonel Ivanovic who came to visit. Now, why I did not know to begin with, but later on I learnt that he tried to convince him that it was just a case of injury, but it wasn't injury, it was -- or self-injury, it was a crime which was unprecedented, and I'm sure things like that will never be seen again, they were so terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what do you know about the killings of Miodrag Saric and Danilo Milincic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Miodrag Saric was killed on the threshold of his own house in Djakovica for the fact that he was a Serb, no other reason, because he didn't want to leave his village and house and move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who exerted pressure on him?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: The Albanian terrorists, exclusively the Albanian terrorists exerted pressure on him to leave. And the Milincic case I know about more, better, because his wife Radmila worked in a school. I helped her get a job as a teacher, and she took part in a rally on the 24th of April in Kosovo Polje. The man was killed in front of his mother's eyes, and before that, in the 1960s, the father was killed and the perpetrator was never uncovered. And we heard how he was killed by Radmila and when the perpetrator was sentenced, she was not even able to follow the trial in the Serbian language. So that's what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm just skimming through these events, which of course upset the public greatly at that time, the attempt to rape the head prioress of the monastery in Devic in 1976, the nun in the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: When Tatjana Todorovic was attacked and raped, the nun that was attacked and raped, unfortunately, on the part of an Albanian, and he was an Albanian policeman, a large number of Serbs and Montenegrins rallied to protested. So it was an act that could not be justified by any count, and I was on the spot. Now the question of the attack on Devic, I also know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: On, rather -- interpreter's correction: On the Mother Superior.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know when Samardzic went to the spot and where the patron saint was Paraskeva with -- she did not have one arm, and the monastery was destroyed several times. It was built in the -- rebuilt in the 14th century, and at the time 90 per cent of the population were Serbs, and since then the monastery has been razed to the ground. This happened, actually, last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. All these events that happened at the time were generally known amongst the public, and you as an inhabitant yourself of Kosovo and Metohija at that time and Kosovo Polje, more specifically, an inhabitant of Kosovo Polje, know about this, but tell me this, please: Did the Albanians start up these mass demonstrations in 1968 and in 1981? Did they launch the demonstrations because they were disenfranchised in any way or were there other reasons?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that they enjoyed every possible right, that then the former Yugoslavia gave them all these rights. It was exclusively a question of having the Serbs and Montenegrins move out and having an ethnically pure Kosovo and then having Kosovo attached to Albania. First of all to proclaim Kosovo a republic and then have it conjoined with Albania. There was no disenfranchisement and as a citizen of Kosovo and Metohija myself I enjoyed far less political, economic, social, material and other rights than did the Albanians, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, I'm going to read to you paragraph 75 of the Kosovo indictment or a portion of that paragraph. This is what it says: "During the 1980s, Serbs voiced concern about discrimination against them by the Kosovo Albanian-led provincial government, led by Kosovo Albanians. While the Kosovo Albanians voiced concern about economic underdevelopment and called for greater political liberalisation and republican status for Kosovo. From 1981 onwards, Kosovo Albanians staged demonstrations, which were suppressed by the SFRY military and police forces of Serbia." My first question for you linked to that quotation is the following: Were the Serbs just discriminated against, as it says here, by the leadership or was terror effected against them?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Not only were Serbs discriminated against, they could have tolerated that some way, but there was terror launched of all kinds and everything that could be used as a means of terror was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's be more specific. When you say all the means of terror, let me ask you this: Did the -- was there physical survival threatened through that terror?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so, because they were killed, raped, their houses taken over, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. We've clarified that point already. Now, tell me this, please: When it says "underdeveloped Kosovo," which is true, Kosovo was indeed the most -- least developed part, what did the other parts of Yugoslavia do to speed up Kosovo's development? Because you were a functionary in the railways at the time, you were a party official, so you were very informed about matters of this kind. But tell me first, were you informed about such matters?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what measures were undertaken?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Let me be allowed to explain this at greater length. Financially speaking, the figure, the figures, the money that was invested I cannot quote, but what I can quote is this: I can tell you what was built and constructed after the war that never existed before the war. I'll probably leave something out, but let me just mention one of the most important things that were built and constructed which shows and reflects how much Yugoslavia, led by Tito, gave the Albanians all their rights, did in Kosovo and Metohija. In Kosovska Mitrovica, for example, there was a battery factory and artificial manure factory that was built. Then we had two large thermoelectric power stations, I don't know their power, but they were built in Obilic. Then there was a nitrogen factory that was built, and a large leather concern, leather factory; a sugar factory; a brewery; a textile factory; a large factory in Urosevac, cables factory; an ammunitions factory in Srbica was built. That is the Drenica municipality. The food and food processing industry was built in Kosovo Polje, an oil industry in Urosevac. So those are just some examples of the construction that was going on and all the factories and everything else that had been built and proves that Yugoslavia invested enormous resources into Kosovo province and it is just not true that the Albanians were economically lagging behind -- that economically they were disenfranchised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija? Were they poorer than the Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija? Did they have more reason to be dissatisfied?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: No. Quite the contrary. The capital in Kosovo and Metohija was largely in the hands of the Albanians. The Serbs were poorer, and they left Kosovo during World War II never to return because they suffered what they had suffered. So they were not richer than the Albanians, they were poorer, except of course there might have been some exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Balevic. Now something else in connection to what I quoted a moment ago where it says the SFRY military and police forces of Serbia suppressed these demonstrations staged. Tell me, please, the police forces of Serbia, did they take part in suppressing the demonstrations at all or could they or, rather, could they have suppressed them?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: The army participated, but let me repeat, at the request of the provincial government. Otherwise, the police forces of Serbia at that time had no right to intervene in Kosovo and Metohija. And there is an official statement made by Minister Lalovic that they mobilised the reserve force three times and let them go three times and waited in a place near Kosovo, but they didn't have the right and authority to enter Kosovo, except when there was an order by the Presidency and when SFRY forces were set up, then the police forces of Serbia, within the composition of those other forces, just like the forces of every other republic, went in to keep law and order and bring law and order back to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, I know you must have told us: During these happenings, where were you and what work were you doing in the 1980s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the 1980s, and I said this -- or, rather, at the end of 1979 to the end of 1984, I was the representative in Bulgaria, but every fortnight I would go back to Pristina and my family continued living in Pristina during that time, if that's the period you're interested in. Everything before and after that period I was in Pristina all the time, in Kosovo all the time. But I had reliable information even then about everything that was going on in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's sum up and be more specific. Were you on the spot when the demonstrations took place in 1981? Because this 1981 year was the year you were in Bulgaria as the representative.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was invited by my family, that is to say my wife and my son Nebojsa, to come back urgently to Pristina because there was chaos there and the danger that -- they were being jeopardised. They said come back straight away, we don't know what to do. I returned the same day when the demonstrations were actually taking place. I had a lot of trouble getting back to my country and back to the place I lived at Merdare because there was police there, and then Podujevo, and then at the Devet Jugovica there was police there too, so I had a lot of trouble in getting through, and I passed not through the centre of town but I passed by the railway station in order to reach my own house so that I was able to follow. I couldn't be in the spot where the demonstrations were, but I was around that area and was able to see what was happening. They were demonstrations bent on destruction, and there was a lot of destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about some other provocations, such as people feigning poisoning, for example, or the miners' strike, or when they were -- the pots and pans they were bashing and banging about, and all this that upset the atmosphere in Kosovo and Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Albanian separatists, helped by the Albanian leadership, thought up all sorts of provocation to draw the attention of the international public about their alleged disenfranchisement and thereby to also exert pressure on the Serbs to flee Kosovo and Metohija. Let me mention the example of the students who feigned food poisoning. This happened during those days. It was ludicrous because you cannot poison anyone on a national ethnic basis. Let me mention the case of the school in Pristina where Milosava Miletic was the assistant headmaster when allegedly an Albanian class of pupils had been poisoned. They left the classroom. She stood before them and said, Don't leave, and she put in some Serb children into the class where the Albanians were allegedly poisoned. So this was all a ludicrous situation, a farce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was said? They were saying that gas was being introduced, leaked into that classroom somehow?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But international experts visited Kosovo and established that there was no such thing, no gas leaks, no poisonings, no poisonous gases, and all that was a fabrication designed to attract the attention of the international public to the so-called terror over Albanians. Second, lighting candles is not an Albanian custom, but they wished to court Catholicism and again to attract attention and support. During those days, processions of people moved through the streets, processions of women with children. Fadil Hoxha and other Albanian leaders were with them, men who used to occupy important offices on the Yugoslav level before that, and they were carrying slogans such as NATO --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Up to 1998, because that's part of the fabrications that were widely mediatised. Then there was this banging of pans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on. We'll come later to 1998, and we won't have to come back again to this particular event that you already explained.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: But let me just add one more thing in response to your question. In the end of the 1980s, Albanians left their workplaces en masse to prove their alleged disenfranchisement before the international community, and they even demanded decisions on their dismissal on paper so that they can produce them and wave them before the international public. Again I also have to mention the strike of the miners in Kosovska Mitrovica, which was completely stage managed, orchestrated, and that was established also about the Communist Party secretary, Stipe Suvar, who went down into the pits to visit the miners and said, Look, you don't look to me like poor miners. And indeed, there were more civilians down there than miners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After those demonstrations in 1980, did the process of the Serb and Montenegrin exodus from Kosovo intensify?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: It did, to the maximum. After -- in the period between 1981 to 1989, 20.000 Serbs and Montenegrins left Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were -- you had a senior position in the railway company, which is a major hub of communications in Kosovo, from Pristina, for a long time. What is your experience with that sort of pressure, harassment, precisely in your job, in the railway company?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I held one of those leading positions, and in the railway traffic, we experienced the same kind of excesses and pressure that jeopardised the safety of railway transport; putting various things on the rails, throwing things at the engineer, people who were driving the trains, endangering the construction of bridges, rupturing of telephone lines and transmission lines. I wrote a very official brief that contains a lot more than I just mentioned in passing here, and I submitted that brief to the minister of the interior. It was later published because I was visited by a Mr. Kordic, a very well known writer, and I told him, by the way, that he has to be very careful because both he and I may end up badly if it is found out where he got his information, and he wrote a book, this Mr. Barjaktarevic containing all that information. I believe the book is in evidence. The safety of railroad traffic was in grave danger, to put it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On a parallel track, what was happening at the same time with the desecration of cultural monuments, Serb or Christian cemeteries in the broadest sense? We had the examples of Bresje, Cabas [phoen], Pod Vitija, Vucitrn.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Bresje used to be my local area where I used to be the president of the regional provincial committees. I visited the place the day after the incident. The photographs on the gravestones were erased. The monuments on the gravestones were toppled, desecrated. I also visited the grave of recently buried babies that had been exhumed. A lot was written about that in the media. I visited the place to check personally. And the other incidents were also confirmed at a meeting in Kosovo Polje that was held on the 24th, 25th April. You can find it in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the forcible eviction and takeover of property?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I have a friend, Mr. Cubranovic, who used to work together with me in the railway company. He was originally from Pec and lived in Guca Gora village. Land was taken from him by force, usurped. Other people worked it without his permission. He reported the incidents, and after spending -- after the perpetrator was sentenced to ten days in gaol, he continued doing the same thing and there was nothing else that could be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said ten days in gaol?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the maximum sentence for usurping land.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the burning of orchards and harvest?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: A lot of information was available about the torching of harvests, wheat and other crops. I can claim with absolute certainty that these things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the policy of employment in Kosovo in those decades, about the so-called principle of national or ethnic representation that was in force then?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: The policy of the Albanian leadership in Kosovo and Metohija was the principle of overwhelming majority. The presentation was at a ratio of 6 to 1 or 7 to 1. In every unit there were six or seven Albanians Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. employed for every Serb that was hired. So Serbs had to wait a long time to get jobs and that was one of the things made them leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Balevic. If I understood you correctly, it didn't matter how qualified or educated you were, how well trained for the job, the only thing that mattered was ethnicity in order to satisfy this principle of ethnic representation, or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: No, you did not misunderstand. In many cases, moreover, the Albanians who were eventually hired were much less trained and less qualified than the Serb candidates. And even the football team that had been branded as Serb had to hire an Albanian player just to make it viable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any personal knowledge about the treatment of Albanian immigrants from Albania from that time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: They were welcomed. They were really cordially welcomed. I don't think they were refugees, I think it was an organised movement from the Albania then led by Enver Hodza. They came on their tractors with their cattle, with their entire luggage, families. Land was given them, land that was sometimes not available, that had to be purchased from the state budget to be given to them, all to the detriment and at the expense of Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Pristina, where you used to live, there was a university where Albanian immigrants from Albania were given spots. Not as students but as lecturers and professors.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Many Albanians who were treated and privileged as refugees whereas in fact they were not were hired by the University of Pristina. Even some Albanian professors, Qosja and others, used to say that they were much lower in qualification than those that had graduated from the university in Pristina. They were hired, nevertheless, but not for the sake of giving them employment. They were hired in order to indoctrinate young Albanians against living together with Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. It's time for the first break. In fact, it's past time. We'll rise for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, do you remember how population censuses were made in Kosovo and Metohija, how the Roma, the Gorani, the Muslims were treated?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President Milosevic, the census of 1971 of 1991 were complete forgeries. For instance, the municipality of Glina, which had 300 Roma houses turned out after the census not to have any. Similar were the cases of the Gorani and others during the censuses. But this is a specific case that proves that censuses were made in such a way to artificially increase the number of Albanians versus the number of Serbs and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that the Roma, Gorani, and others were shown as Albanians during the censuses?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, in order to deteriorate the ethnic structure of Kosovo and Metohija to the benefit of Albanians and to the detriment of Serbs, Montenegrins, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the pressures exerted on non-Albanians in various companies and enterprises?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: There was a lot of pressure of every kind in the course of bilingual administration and bureaucracy. For instance, various papers and decisions were written and issued to Serbs in Albanian which they couldn't read. At various sessions, meetings of the electorate or their working staff were held in Albanian. There was interpretation provided in some cases, in others not, and the message to Serbs was, "What are you looking for here? You should leave."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did Serbs, Montenegrins, and others -- other non-Albanians have equal treatment in medical institutions? Could they feel safe?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not, and I'll give you an example to prove this. The maternity clinic in Pristina, led at the time by Mrs. Mekuli, wife of the famous Albanian writer Mr. Mekuli, where newborns of Serb and Montenegrin ethnicity died en masse after delivery, because Serb and Montenegrin mothers were forced to stop labour there and go to neighbouring towns like Skopje, Prokuplje, Nis, and others. The head of the maternity ward behaved in a way that I will try to illustrate with an example, an example that shows that Serb and Montenegrin women were right to doubt her ethics. During the demonstrations of 1981, there were people injured, and she told them, upon meeting them, "Congratulations on your wounds, heroes." And since it was decided that it was dangerous to send women to that clinic for delivery, it was decided further to build a maternity clinic in Kosovo Polje in 1987. However, once it was built and the foundations were ceremonially opened by Minister Todorovic, it was decided to use it for another purpose. It never became a maternity clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Kosovo Polje is one of the few settlements that are purely Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the percentage of Serb residents in Kosovo Polje at the time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, there were more than 60 per cent Serbs in Kosovo Polje and in the surrounding villages Dobri Dug, Nakarade and so on, Albanians lived. But over 60 per cent of residents in Kosovo Polje were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the personnel policy in Kosovo Polje now that we're dealing with your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, unfortunately, the personnel policy was contrary to the ethnic composition and the composition of residents in Kosovo Polje. I will give you an example. The director of abattoir was Avdi Musa, an Albanian from Podujevo, which is some 40 kilometres from Kosovo Polje. When he was appointed to that post, he brought with him some 40 Albanian workers. They came to work in the factory so as to change the ethnic composition of the factory workers. The director of the cattle farm was also an Albanian. Another factory director was from Pec. I do not remember his name. The director of Zitopromet was also an Albanian, Esmeti Fablia [phoen], and the other one whose name I couldn't remember was called Feta Gravci [phoen]. The director of ZTP in Kosovo Polje was first Zenun Beqaj, an Albanian; and then Xheladin Sahiti, also an Albanian. So that most industrial enterprises except for the pig-raising farm, which was headed by a Serb because an Albanian did not want to occupy that post, were led by Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about toponyms and place names and Cyrillic script used for those place names?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were various requests lodged by Albanian nationalists aimed at ensuring that the churches are marked in the same ways as mosques. The names of towns were changed in the entire Kosovo and Metohija. For example, Urosevac was called Ferizaj, Dzeneral Jankovic was called Hani I Elezit, Dobra Voda was called Ujmiri, Kosovo Polje Fushe Kosova, and what is interesting to note is that there was a debate which name should be placed first, the Albanian or the Serbian one. They requested that the Albanian name go first because Albanians had majority in Kosovo and Metohija. However, Serbs resisted this and they applied a horizontal principle which was not so easy to enforce. So it was a mixed situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were an official at the time, please tell us, did the authorities in Kosovo and Metohija show readiness and intention to prevent terror against Serbs and Montenegrins and other non-Albanian residents? Did they attempt to prevent the pressure to have these people leave?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, had the state leadership and the party leadership of Kosovo and Metohija wanted to prevent everything, had this leadership wanted to prevent everything that was happening, there would not have been any exodus of Serb and Montenegrin and other residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell me, did the state and party organs condemn the terror that was being carried out against Serbs and Montenegrins and other non-Albanians in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Some leaders did condemn it verbally, but just to show you how strong that condemnation was, these people in fact supported the adoption of the law banning the return of Serbs and Montenegrins. They allowed the name of Kosovo and Metohija to be changed in Kosovo only. They also supported the 1974 constitution, they supported the introduction of an Albanian flag, and so on, so what kind of support they could have given to the cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You Serbs from Kosovo and Metohija, did you bear in mind that the Republic of Serbia had a constitutional obligation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The audio feed was cut off for a minute. Could Mr. Milosevic please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're being asked to repeat the question because the audio feed was cut off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I see that my mike is on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you Serbian and Montenegrin residents of Kosovo and Metohija, did you know that the Republic of Serbia was constitutionally duty-bound to protect your rights and freedoms because you were Serbian citizens?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: As was stated in the constitution, Serbia was supposed to intervene. However, its authorities in that old constitution were limited. Despite that, Serbia could have intervened with the federal organs and provincial organs to prevent this. However, its constitutional authorities were quite limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you about is whether you were aware of that. Did you know that Serbia had no executive or judicial authorities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we knew that because -- we knew that Serbia had no authorities in the province, however, Serbs and Montenegrins expected Serbia to do something, to take some measures to save what was possible to save in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please explain to us, how did it come about that Serbs and Montenegrins engaged in this self-organisation in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Well, first we started with various gatherings in 1981 and 1983 in Kosovo Polje, Prelluzhe, Vucitrn, Pec, Gnjilane, Gracanica, and so on. Throughout Kosovo various gatherings were held. There were many delegations which went to federal organs which agreed to see them. So this was a mass movement undertaken by Serbs and Montenegrins from Kosovo who sought solution for their problems and who wanted Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo and Metohija to be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you went to speak with various highly placed officials. Therefore, please tell us, what politicians at the federal republican and provincial level, at the level of the province of Kosovo, saw these delegations of Serbs and Montenegrins from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the first delegation went to visit Nikola Ljubicic, who at the time was the president of the Presidency. I think that we can find the date if that is needed. Therefore a delegation of Serbs and Montenegrins went to see him. He greeted them rather poorly. It would have been better had they not gone there. He showed no understanding for the problems of Serbs and Montenegrins. Then the second delegation, which was not really a delegation but a large assembly of people, went to see Bozo Markovic at the Assembly. There they met Ilijaz Kurteshi, who was the president of the Federal Assembly. They did not want to go and speak to him, and they had good reasons for that, because it was precisely the Albanian leadership that had expelled them from Kosovo. I think that they saw Lazar Mojsov and Bogdan Trifunovic. They talked to them. And Bozo Markovic said at the time, "You cannot lead these people in this state. I have to lead them." And this is when that famous sentence was uttered, "Your children have peaceful sleep. I want my children to sleep peacefully at night as well." Lazar Mojsov said to these people not a hair on your head should be harmed. And when these Serbs and Montenegrins returned to Kosovo, the terror continued despite of the assurances received from Lazar Mojsov.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you have any positive examples that you can quote now?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was just about to say that. They visited Patriarch German, who showed understanding for their cause. They asked for his blessing. In addition, they went to Dusan Ckrebic, and he assured them he would do everything that was possible to ensure that Serbs and Montenegrins remain in Kosovo and Metohija and are spared from terror. A group of 16 intellectuals, including Jago Zelenovic, Odalovic, Moravcic, and so on, visited Milanko Renovica, who was the president of the Presidency of the Central Committee of the League of Communists for Yugoslavia, to seek help to protect Serbdom, to ensure that Serbs remained living in Kosovo and Metohija and are spared from terror. He did not show much understanding. Therefore, Ckrebic was the only positive experience. These intellectuals, upon their return to Kosovo and Metohija, had a lot a problems with the security organs, such as Jago Zelenovic and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who were the members of those delegations of Serbs and Montenegrins from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this group of intellectuals, everybody who was in the position to join the delegation went. In some delegations there were even several Albanian members. There were some Albanians in certain delegations, however, they did not want to publicise their presence and participation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of any delegation?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I was in a delegation where there were about 15 members who visited Dizdarevic. He was the president of the Presidency. This was a delegation whose arrival was -- had been announced. There were a lot of problems in arranging that meeting. We arrived at around 10.00 p.m., his Chief of Staff met us, told us that Dizdarevic would see us but we needed to wait. We told him we didn't want to see the Chief of Staff but wanted to see Dizdarevic himself. Later on he did meet with us. There were some 15 of us in that delegation, 15 of us Serbs. Although he already knew a lot, we told him about the sufferings and the plight of the Serbs and Montenegrins. We told him that there were 15.000 people waiting for us in front of the culture hall in Kosovo Polje to see what were the results of the meeting. He promised that he would help us, he would undertake measures. I would like to point out that one member of the delegation, Ljubo Vujovic asked him then, "Comrade President, what needs to happen for the army of Yugoslavia to intervene in Kosovo and Metohija to prevent what is happening to the Serbs?" And he told him if the army cannot arrive at the spot within half an hour, then it's too late. We returned to Kosovo Polje early in the morning. We conveyed the information that we heard and told them about the talks we had with Dizdarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As far as I remember - and you can correct me if I'm wrong - my impression was that you had a very positive assessment of the treatment you received in that meeting with Raif Dizdarevic.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our impression was just as you said; that he showed understanding, that he said he would take measures, and that he had a -- he was -- he had a Yugoslav orientation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. There were many of these delegations, some numbering a lot of members, and these delegations felt -- met with a lot of politicians and there were also a lot of politicians that came to your communities and spoke to the people there.
