Is that right or not? I remember, for example, that Drnovsek, president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, came to visit you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I probably will not be able to list those visits chronologically, but I will try to remember the names who came to Pristina and Kosovo Polje. President of the Presidency, Ivan Stambolic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think we need that level of detail. We don't need that level of detail for this background matter. You may consider that you can move fairly quickly through these background matters, which, concededly, are referred to in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, please tell us, the Serbs and Montenegrins held protest gatherings, rallies. Could you tell us something about them.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Judge just told me not to go over these visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We don't need to go into details, that is not the most important information.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Serbs and Montenegrins held protest rallies, gatherings. Could you tell us when and where they were held, and tell us whether these protest rallies and gatherings were peaceful or violent.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends on a case-by-case basis, depending on what excesses and crimes had committed. Initially these gatherings were held indoors. However, if more strong condemnation was in place, such as after the events in Divaca [phoen] and so on, then rallies and gatherings were held out in the open, in front of schools and large buildings and so on. But I can tell you that all gatherings that were held in the area where I was present, no incidents ever took place during those rallies. Everything was conducted with dignity. And these rallies were a last resort for the Serbs and Montenegrins fighting for their survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We could say that you have a very important role because you were one of the organisers, and you personally were a host at --

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question, because I didn't hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was saying, we'll get to some specific questions, which are very important ones in view of the fact that you were one of the organisers yourself and that you were a host to the meetings and rallies held in Kosovo Polje, first of all on the 20th and then on the 24th, between the 24th and 25th of April, 1987. So before I ask you my question with respect to those meetings and rallies, I'm going to read out to you. It is paragraph 76 of the Kosovo indictment, which states the following: "In April 1987, Slobodan Milosevic, who had been elected as Chairman of the Presidium of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Serbia in 1986, travelled to Kosovo. The meetings with the local Serb leaders and in a speech before a crowd of Serbs, Slobodan Milosevic endorsed a Serbian nationalist agenda. In so doing, he broke with the party and government policy, which had restricted nationalist expression in the SFRY since the time of its founding by Josip Broz Tito after the Second World War. Thereafter, Slobodan Milosevic exploited a growing wave of Serbian nationalism in order to strengthen centralised rule in the SFRY." Let us go back for a moment to this. What it says here is that Slobodan Milosevic directly supported and endorsed the Serbian nationalist programme, or agenda, as it says here. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender an exhibit now. It is entitled Sleepless Nights, and it is the transcript from these meetings and rallies in April, first of all on the 20th, and then between the 24th and 25th of April. And, Mr. Robinson, from this book there are some 37 pages that have been pinpointed, and Professor Rakic sent them to be translated. The translation into English is not yet available, so I shall just be quoting briefly from certain passages that have not been translated. Some of them have been translated, and they accompany a tape that I'm going to play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When did you send them in for translation, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation was requested -- well, I can't give you an exact date, but it was sometime towards the end of December. And in any case, sufficient time, sufficiently early on for it to be translated prior to these proceedings here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The end of December. I don't think that would be sufficient lead time in accordance with the administrative practice, but you may put it on the -- what do you plan to do? Do you plan to read these short passages?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I intend to read several passages, only a few passages from what has not been translated, whereas the portion relating to the rally itself at which allegedly, as it says in this paragraph, in 77, I supported the nationalist agenda, you have that on the tape. And there is a translation to follow the tape. So I think that's all in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can read some short passages. It will be translated. But I don't want you to read for long periods. Read a passage and then you're going to ask the witness to comment on it. You didn't tell us who authored Sleepless Nights.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sleepless Nights was the book of transcripts. The author of the book is Radojica Barjaktarevic, and the book was published in 1995, and it contains everything that took place at the rally held on the 24th and 25th of April and the previous meeting. But let's take things one by one in order. Before I read out any passages at all, let me ask the witness this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, I came to Kosovo Polje on the 20th of April myself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who invited me to come to Kosovo Polje in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: You were invited to come to Kosovo Polje by the Serbs and Montenegrins from Kosovo and Metohija. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, was it envisaged, since you invited me, that a meeting of some kind be held with the representatives of the Serbs and Montenegrins of Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: For the situation to be clearer with respect to the meeting, Mr. President, may I be allowed to state this: The first meeting that was held prior to the other meeting was the one held on the 16th of April, 1987, and it was held in front of Dr. Zoran Grujic's house. And he wrote a letter to all the organs, federal organs and municipal organs, that he was leaving Kosovo with his family and relations because of the terror exerted against his family and the persecution. And because of the letter he had sent with those contents, a large group of Serbs and Montenegrins rallied together in front of his house. I went to the rally as president of the regional conference, because it -- the relay baton race was to be run, the traditional relay baton race was to be run through those parts. So I went there and I asked the people to dissemble peacefully. They agreed to do so only when I had promised that we would invite the president of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, who was Slobodan Milosevic at the time, to come to Kosovo Polje himself. And we wrote to the president of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Serbia. It could have been some other person, some other Milosevic, but you were there, you happened to be there, so we invited to you come. You accepted our invitation, and I promised that a meeting of the Serbs - and there were too many to be held in a hall - that they be held somewhere else, that is to say in front of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you have answered the question sufficiently. The point is clear. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So when I arrived, you had planned to have a meeting and a rally to evoke the problems that you were facing and that were troubling the citizens and inhabitants of Kosovo. And you first thought that the meeting would be held in the hall of the railway company.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why wasn't it held in the railway company hall?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: That was impossible, because the people, the citizens, the Serbs and Montenegrins, learnt of your arrival, that you would be coming, although we kept it secret until the late afternoon, but people got to hear about it, that you would come to the area, and then it was impossible to have thousands of citizens accommodated in that hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that the hall was too small because there were several thousand people that wanted to take part and the hall was too small; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So where did we all go then? They were in front -- they had met in front of the railway building, the railway station, in fact, so where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: We went to the Aca Marovic primary school building, where you delivered a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm just going to read out one passage from the speech I delivered on the 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's on page 66 of the B/C/S text in the book. That is a collection of all these speeches, and it comes under one heading called Sleepless Nights published by the author Radojica Barjaktarevic. I'm going to read the last paragraph of that speech of mine. I say: "Comrades, the problems --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... overhead projector. I'm sorry to be so technical, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- who read the language to follow it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. That's a very good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, would you be kind enough to turn to page 66 now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could the usher place this page on the overhead projector, but Mr. Balevic has the book in front of him. And I can hand you a copy myself. Can you find page 66 and then place it on the overhead projector. It is the paragraph before the heading "The people are electing their delegates." The usher will help us out and place it on the ELMO. Is that it? Can we take a look? It's at the top of the page. Fine. That's the paragraph I wish to quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Comrades, the problems in Kosovo can be resolved only if we strengthen the front of the Serbs, Montenegrins and Albanians and all the other nations and nationalities living in Kosovo who are capable of effecting those changes. It should be strengthened not because we wish to realise a principled slogan about brotherhood and unity. The slogan of brotherhood and unity in Kosovo has its foundations in the fact that it is in the best interests of all the inhabitants of Kosovo to have Kosovo develop speedily, successfully, regardless of whether they are a Serb, a Montenegrin or Albanian or whether they belong to some other nationality or ethnic group or some other ethnicity or nation. That, Comrades, is the material basis upon which we must realise the programme of the League of Communists pertaining to Kosovo. And, ladies and gentlemen, that is the groundwork that we're going to be victorious on. Any other foundations based on national intolerance and the dissemination of national hatred cannot be a progressive basis for communists and the League of Communists itself. Socialist Yugoslavia can solve the problem of Kosovo only on the platform of brotherhood and unity and national equality. And that is how it will indeed be resolved." So is that then the substance of what I said when I addressed those many people that had rallied in the courtyard on the 20th of April, the courtyard of the Aca Marovic school in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am asking you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the substance. Yes, that is the substance of it, the substance of what you said in Kosovo Polje. And I think that any comment here is superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is no need. I'm just asking you, was that authentic? Is that what I said?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is authentic. That is what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then we decided that in the space of several days, a meeting and a rally would be held where you and your delegates would be elected and given the floor to present the troubles and problems they were facing. Is that what we had decided at that Kosovo Polje meeting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Now, this brings me to another rally, the meeting that was organised pursuant to that agreement, and that subsequent meeting was held -- actually, it began in the late afternoon of the 24th of April and ended on the 25th of April; is that right? Is that right, Mr. Balevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It lasted for about 13 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, who chaired or presided over that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I as the president of the Regional Conference of the League of Communists of Kosovo Polje, and my name is Mitar Balevic. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Now, I come to another passage that has not yet been translated, so I'll read just a few sentences out. It is from the introductory remarks made by you as the chairman of the meeting, and this is what you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 91 and goes on to page 93 of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you plan to read 91 to 93?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. No. A passage is highlighted on page 91, and it is four lines, and then on page 93 a few more lines, but they have been highlighted, and I am bearing in mind the fact that in point 76, it says that I endorsed a Serbian nationalist agenda at the time, and now the chairman who was there at the time put forward a nationalist programme that I supported. And I'm going to quote what Mr. Balevic said at that time, and you will find it on page 91. This is what he says: "The political security situation in the region is burdened by -- makes it difficult or is burdened by hostile positions, especially Albanian nationalism and irredentism and the continued exodus of Serbs and Montenegrins. The activities of the bourgeois right hand movement and fanning the flames of nationalism, and goes on to speak of the difficult economic situation," et cetera, et cetera, and I'll leave out that next passage. And now we come to page 93. There's just a portion of the sentence, the first sentence on page 92. It says: "We have greater knowledge and consciousness with the leading working people and citizens of all the nations and nationalities as to the detriments and dangers that nationalism present." And then in the next paragraph we have the following: They speak about the struggle against all nationalisms and then says: "Our nations and nationalities' options as well as those of all the citizens of working class in the region to persevere and live together in the area under the skies," et cetera, et cetera. And then it says: "This was confirmed by the relay baton that was -- that passed by in 1987 and it was the symbol of brotherhood and unity wherein lies our strength." And then he says: "I'm convinced that through the discussions we're going to have now and in the future we'll continue along that road because we cannot digress from Tito's road and Tito's course." That is what Mr. Balevic said. He's sitting here with us now and this is allegedly supposed to be some Serbian nationalist agenda which I allegedly supported at that rally, whereas in actual fact what I read out and what Mr. Balevic said I assume clearly denies any ideas of any kind of nationalist agenda here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... reading the passage but I think the comments should be reserved for another time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Fine, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, I've read out several passages from your speech. Now, what you said at the time, was it any kind of Serbian nationalist programme or agenda?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is ludicrous to observe that what I said at that rally, that it can be called Serbian nationalism. It seems that we have put things topsy-turvy there because there's not a single word or any idea of Serb nationalism at all, because I appeal to brotherhood and unity and those sentiments. I even quoted President Tito. So any other comment is superfluous. We're not dealing with any kind of Serbian nationalism. Then if you did so, you would have to proclaim that all the Serbs that were in Kosovo were in favour of Serb nationalism, which is a ludicrous idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I said in fact, Mr. Milosevic, I believe there's a passage in which the witness warned against the dangers of nationalism. Is that so, Mr. Balevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. I cautioned against those dangers, and I warned that we would also fight against Serb nationalism wherever it appears. But it cannot be interpreted as an expression of Serb nationalism here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What prompted you to make that caution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What prompted me was the fear that some Serb nationalism -- nationalists could show up and abuse our rally and endanger our brotherhood and unity in Kosovo Polje, because at that time on that occasion we are condemning any attempts at expressing Serb nationalism. Which doesn't mean to say that this particular speech contains a single word of Serb nationalism or that there was anything of that kind for Mr. Milosevic to support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]
