utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The rally scheduled for Monday was supposed to include 300 people selected to attend a citizens' assembly of Kosovo Polje scheduled for Monday. For the most part they were representatives of the population of Kosovo Polje and the surrounding villages. "When Slobodan Milosevic, president of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Serbia, Azem Vllasi, Kolj Siroka, a member of the Presidency of the Central Committee for Yugoslavia, accompanied by provincial leaders arrived in Kosovo Polje at 6.00 p.m., some 15.000 citizens had assembled in front of the cultural hall. As soon as the meeting began an incident took place when the police using truncheons attempted to drive the mass away from the cultural hall. Citizens reacted by throwing back stones and hard objects. The person presiding over the Assembly in the hall then asked Slobodan Milosevic to step out and make an appeal to the citizens in front of the cultural hall. Under such conditions, no dialogue was possible. Loudspeakers were put on the window and Slobodan Milosevic addressed people from the window." "Mr. Milosevic: Comrades, we have to work to hear out all your delegates. Under the circumstances, we will be discussing what you have entrusted your people to say. Do, however, allow us to hold a meeting, not a rally. There will be no use from any rallies. But we can agree about a meeting. "Anchorman: After an interruption of half an hour, another hundred delegates entered into the hall coming mainly from other places in Kosovo. The citizens from other places started to disperse whereas talks in the hall continued throughout the night. "Darinka Popovic: I want to live here where I was born. I want my children to continue living here. I want them to visit my grave. I don't want to go to Serbia. If I have to go, I'd rather die. "Zivojin Ristic: I live in a village where there are only four Serbian houses with a total of 13 persons. In '77, with four children and my wife, I started to build a house that I inherited from my grandfather, father, uncle, on the land that they left me. In '62, '63, when we started building that small house, every night, every two -- every second or third night our old house was stoned. This was reported to the police. Nonetheless, it was repeated. It went on. One night they opened the window above my head and here in the room in which we were sitting five, six stones landed. "Kata Komatina: All these problems are here. All has been said. There is nothing else to say. We need to start doing something. We can't say, come off now, we'll do something tomorrow. We need to do something now, immediately. We should know or let our people know what's going to happen to them, whether they are Serbs, Albanians, Turks. It doesn't matter who they are. They are Yugoslav people on this territory. The people know where -- need to know where they are. We don't want any more drifting. Why do we have all these political structures? Why do we have all these people leading us? Why do we elect incompetent good for nothings while other people are forcing this mass to turn around in circles? We can't allow for this any more. "Milanko Buljugic: They evicted me twice from Kosovo. I returned twice. When they tried to chase me away, they couldn't manage, but now, using this method, I will go on my own. Comrades, Comrade Slobodan Milosevic, if greater employment possibilities existed in Serbia, you would then really be able to see what the situation is really like today here, but naturally people don't move because where will they find work? This explains why the rhythm of exodus has been slower than it could be. "One of the major principled issues for us here, it is a vital question, is the problem of legal equality and legal safeguards or, rather, inequality and the lack of legal safeguards. The republic and the federal Yugoslav leadership are -- had enough information about this. They know everything. Three thick volumes exist containing the findings of various working groups pertaining to illegal activities. But Comrades, they can always say, well, it's all right, in other places the law is also not fully observed. That is correct, Comrades, but it's like a bikini. A bikini shows you a lot but it hides the most important things. What are we talking about? It's true that the law is not respected in other places as well but let us look into why it is being violated here. "Mirko Cupic: Those who have ignited the fire cannot extinguish it. You cannot let the wolf look after the sheep. People who through their opportunism or their impetus or with their direct instigation of ideological diversity cannot put out this fire. A number of young Albanians, despite the fact that they are pro-Yugoslav, cannot raise their heads because of older political officials, though they don't want to admit it. Neither the Serb nor the Montenegrin people here are against Albanians or the Albanian people. "Voice from the public: That's true. "They never have been, but the Serbian people is against the separatist movement which wants to establish an ethnically pure Kosovo, and by way of an ethnically pure Kosovo, to destroy this country. And they will achieve this if these actions continue as they have to date. "Stevan Marinkovic: The leaders of the federal autonomous province of Kosovo are applying parts of the constitution of Serbia as they interpret them whereas the leaders of Serbia do not apply parts of the constitution of Serbia as they interpret them on the entire territory of the republic. What am I then to say? To whom do I then belong? If any of you should like to take part in the discussion, I should wish the audience to understand this. Citizens who belong to the Serbian and Montenegrin peoples are particularly affected by the different interpretation of those parts of the constitution of Serbia which pertain to security, defence, the legal system, et cetera. But Albanians separatists see this situation as strengthening the statehood of the province of Kosovo and weakening of Serbia which coincides entirely with their strategy of achieving statehood for Kosovo and they know it's merely a question of time. We already had the opportunity in 1991 to see this with our own eyes, and ever since, it's been the same. But what comes after this statehood, where are we? "Boro Dzelektovic: To remain here, to live together with Albanians so as to achieve this, to remain here, that which we have lost has to be restituted to us. What is that? That is Comrades, Comrade President, justice, freedom, script, culture and language. This should be returned to us and then we will remain here. But Comrade President, I did not come here neither did this honest people come here so as to seek greater rights than other citizens of our country who live within the borders of our homeland. Rather, we came here to become equals and to live together in brotherhood and unity with all peoples and nationalities who live on the territory of Kosovo. That is that. "Daut Bogujevci: This evening I hear such insults directed at the Albanian people, saying Albanian peasants are not dangerous. We have leaders. We have educated people. Please, is it so? Are they at fault? When Albanian nationalism burst forth, honest Albanian communists were the first in line to repel these Albanian nationalists or condemn them. Excuse me, please. I know this. I'm an activist here. I'm also here, I'm an activist. "Voice from the public: Time is up. "No, time is not up. I'm the only Albanian to be speaking here. I have the right to speak more. "Voice from the public: Please have patience. "I see here tonight that certain discussions in reality are misplaced here and have no logic whatsoever. To tell you the truth, Comrade President, many tombstones have been destroyed in my village. You heard this in the press, in the village of Bresje. Please, I insist that as an Albanian many times that these facts be made public and they reveal who is destroying the tombstones. I want to tell you one thing: I think the enemy is known. Only those tombstones belonging to the poor have been destroyed whereas the colossal ones have not been touched. Here things are reported. Everybody in this country has a last name and a first name. I want it to be said that Daut Bogujevci is such and such person, he committed this particular crime. I don't think that peoples' reputation should be sullied in such a general way. Today every word has a certain weight. Everybody knows where it is headed, what it is aimed at. Today nobody's stupid. Please. We were very poor. We were all poor. I want to tell you that here, in my village, Bresje, we from the Bogujevci family have 16 unemployed members whereas in the entire village there are just three or four unemployed. Everybody else is employed and they were never richer. "Radomir Kapetanovic: To tell you the truth, when I decided to come here I intended to remain silent for 15 minutes so that my silence be a speech to you because sometimes silence speaks volumes. I've been speaking up in my working organisation, in my basic organisation, in the League of Communists for ten years, and the effect is the same; as though I've been talking to the walls. I wanted and asked to be held responsible if the facts I brought up were inaccurate without verifying my facts. I, together with my words, was placed ad acta. To this day, I'm a member of the League of Communists. I hope I shall so remain despite the fact that certain high officials who are present have for years been forcing me out to the sidelines and have been doing all they can so as to discredit me by removing me from the League of Communists. Not because I'm wrong, not because I'm a nationalist, Comrades, only because I'm a thorn in the side in the department of chemistry and the faculty for Albanian separatists, who unfortunately are very numerous. This meeting must be perceived as a cry for help. I reiterate, a cry for help for the elementary rights to life and to work. Those to whom this cry is directed at must not remain deaf. We all came here, something I can guarantee you for myself, for the good of Yugoslavia, and it has occurred to no one to attain a higher position by depriving others of their rights. I desire no rights at the cost of injustice towards others. I shall be ashamed of all those who desire positions in order to deprive others of their rights. The League of Communists must - the verb 'must' is a strong one - but it must value the fact that the people are making an appeal to it. This is the proof that the people believe in the party. This is the proof that the people believe in the party and we are turning to you, Comrade President, to you in the first place as a member of the League of Communists, as the president of the Central Committee of Serbia. "Miroslav Solevic: Well, we shall stop this. Either it will start going, flowing back so that the people may return to their hearths or we shall collectively depart. There is no dilemma. We ask you, Comrade President, to tell to the leaders of Serbia that the leaders of Serbia tell the Yugoslav leadership that they need to give us a clear answer. This is what we are requesting. We want to live here. This is our basic wish, but not in this way, no. We want to live here. We want to respect order and work both in this country and in this province. All residents of this province have to, irrespective of their nationality, live from their work and not from the help received from the federation. We are not blind people. The province not poor. It's not true. "Milica Aleksic: In the Podujevo Municipal Assembly discussions have taken place about the moving out of Serbs and Montenegrins. In the documents which were submitted to the delegates and the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly in charge of preparing the documents, wrote that a perfidious moving out of Serbs and Montenegrins had taken place in the Podujevo municipality. I opened up the encyclopedia to see -- to see what that term "perfidiousness" meant. It said that it meant cunning, malice. I met with the vice-president of the municipality and asked him, please, Comrade Serif, tell me why have 33 Serbian families moved out of your village? Was it done in order to arm the honest Albanians, to say, look, they evicted Serbs and Montenegrins? "Jovanka Vukovic: Comrade Milosevic, I would only like to ask you whether somebody will be held responsible for the Serbian children in this province for the dirty acts that have been committed? Will anybody be held responsible for that? And the comrades who they are referred to me as a sword in somebody else's hands, I would like to say that, no, I'm just a woman with her own sufferings. I have survived tragic events which few mothers could live through. This is why I attempted to remove my one child from here. These are difficult moments because of what I said, because I expressed my honest opinion, my right and truthful words, by which I still stand. I was called a sword in somebody's hands. In whose hands? Had I known at the time, believe me, I would have irrespective of whose hands were in question been only there where I can have rights. I have no rights in this province, and I'm not going to take up any more time, but just will say to you give us freedom here or send us to Serbia to get freedom there. "Dusica Zoric: Comrades, I beg you, you who are in the first row, to put yourselves in the position of those who have come here in order to express their problems. Why don't you take the floor and speak of your problems and let the people who have voiced their problems be in your seats? Would you have asked for a concrete responsibility? I think that you would have. Therefore, under the circumstances, I ask that you understand us. We are people facing problems. During the previous mandate, I was a representative in the federal parliament, in the federal council. As a representative, as a delegate, I did my best to express what problems we had, to speak of these people. I understand that every problem, whether it involves the Serbs, the Montenegrins, the Albanians, Turks, the Gorani, or members of another nation or nationality is particularly difficult and requires full attention. But Comrades, if we demand that every problem be analysed separately, that is too vast a task even for the courts. At meetings such as this one, we should focus concretely on those problems which led to such massive violations of the constitution and the laws, the problems which will lead to, which have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. already led to the situations where we have many problems in Yugoslavia. We have Kosovo. We have an economic situation which is difficult. We have an inflation, ramping inflation. We have many problems, and it is high time that we had some unity. "Anchor: After 13 hours of uninterrupted talks, this morning around 7.00 Slobodan Milosevic took the floor. "Slobodan Milosevic: Comrades, before I say a few words about the substance of our today's discussions, I would like to say that there is no need for us to trade places as the lady said just a moment ago in order to ask for accountability. It is our duty. "And as for the unfortunate incident that happened here today and the police intervention that ensued, the responsibility for this intervention for which there was no reason will be established. This is completely clear. "Comrade Mitar, our chairman today, informed us about what was happening in front of the building, and you know quite well that within one minute we agreed that it is not -- that it should not be the police maintaining order but that you should undertake that yourselves in the interests of the safety of citizens and children who were there. The proof that it was the right decision was the fact that order was maintained quite well and that people behaved with dignity. "Now, finally, I would like to say something about the substance of our talks. I would like to say something about how such gatherings are evaluated, qualified. To put it briefly, these gatherings are not the gatherings of nationalists. They are not the gatherings of enemies either. And precisely because of that, Comrades, and I know that the vast majority of those who are present here and those outside of it will side with me on this, that we must not allow such gatherings of citizens to be abused by nationalists. All honest people have to stand up against this, because we must guard our brotherhood and unity like the apple of our eye. This is the only way. Especially nowadays when the brotherhood and unity are threatened. We must and we can win. "We neither wish nor we can classify people into Serbs and Albanians, but we should distinguish among the honest and progressive people fighting for brotherhood and unity and national equality on the one hand and nationalists and counter-revolutionaries on the other hand. If we do not create and strengthen that front, Comrades, then there will be no Kosovo, no Serbia, and no Yugoslavia either. "Another issue that I would like to bring up is this: I want to assure you that all the problems that you have discussed here, literally every word will be conveyed to the members of the Central Committee of the Communist League of Serbia. They will be told about it not just for the purpose of informing them but in order to solve the problems within the institutional framework of our system. I had to say this in the beginning since it is physically impossible to discuss all of the questions that have been brought up here. "Comrades, everybody in entire Yugoslavia is aware of the fact that Kosovo is a great problem of our society, which is being resolved very slowly. However, I have to say that if Kosovo had been the only problem, or at least the only major problem of the Yugoslavia society, the issues would have been solved faster and better. However, the problem in Kosovo occurred at the same time as the great economic crisis when the standard of living drastically deteriorated, when prices went up and the rate of unemployment grew. There are also political problems. You are aware of the fact that our country has been shaken by separatism and nationalism in many parts although not to such an extent as here in Kosovo. "And finally, there have been increasingly present aggressive anti-Yugoslav and anti-communist forces. Thus at the same time when there were many serious problems, our society and the League of Communists have a lot of problems they are dealing with, and this is why the solution is difficult to find. "The League of Communists has not always been united in solving all of these problems. Therefore, they could not be sufficiently efficient. I do not bring this up as a justification since I'm not entitled to but as a statement. The request for unity is the most important task facing the party today. This request that there be unity was mentioned in every speech at the session of the Serbian Central Committee recently held. I'm convinced that we have made a large step forward, moving into the direction of the unity of both the Serbian Central Committee and the Yugoslav League of Communists. Only united can we solve many problems, and if we're not united we can solve none of them. "Despite many of the measures some of which you have mentioned as having been taken particularly in the past year, the situation in Kosovo, both the economic and political situation, continues to be dissatisfactory. Kosovo continues to be underdeveloped. There is a lot of unemployment. We have a lot of foreign debts. Exports are not satisfactory. We have a lot of buildings that have -- where construction hasn't been finished and there is great abuse of work and the function of administration in various services, and this includes the realm of politics as well. "We discussed this problems today both at the Presidency meeting, and I can tell you that that was yesterday at the Presidency meeting of the Provincial Committee, these problems were raised. It was held yesterday at noon. We discussed these issues, and we also discussed the question of education and upbringing, cadres policy, and that that -- there was still a spirit of separatism and very often counter-revolutionary spirit prevailing there too. The fact that the Serbs and Montenegrins are leaving the area under economic, political and physical pressure, this, too, represents the last tragic exodus of the population in Europe, and the last time such processions of desperate people were seen was in the Middle Ages. "I know full well that you need not listen to stories of what happened in the past or just to have an analysis of the present situation. Nobody is interested in that any more. And that is quite logical, because you and all of us are interested and should be interested only in those agreements who -- which will be able to change things for the better, which can resolve the situation we are all in, all of us together, you and then all of us together. But I do, nonetheless, wish to assure you that many measures have been taken in the field of financial/political relations, personnel policies, and that they are changing daily and that those changes will be even faster in the months to come. "The material development of Kosovo is something that is constantly being invested in. Separatism and nationalism have been treated as a counter-revolution, and there are substantial changes in personnel, policies, legal, administrative, ideological, and political measures are being put forward, but nobody is satisfied at the rate at which this is going, this process, neither in the Provincial Committee or in the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Serbia or Yugoslavia. And we observed that yesterday at the meeting of the Presidency that was held. However, the process is gaining acceleration, and I am convinced that it will be even faster in the times to come, and that is something that I wish to assure you of. "However, we must understand from this, and I don't want to imply or suggest a solution and say that we have any reason to be satisfied. Quite the contrary. Kosovo is still today the poorest part of our country and the Albanian separatists and nationalists seem to have calmed down somewhat. They think time is on their side. And of course circumstances are in their favour, too, but let them know this: They should know that on this territory, there will be no tyranny. The progressive people of Kosovo will not allow it. Neither will Serbia or Yugoslavia allow it. "As for politics, in the political view, we still have the idea that the request for an ethnically pure Kosovo is justified and possible, and that's where the crux of the matter lies, because it is from this kind of attitude whereby the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo is considered to be a socio-political community of the Albanian nationality in Kosovo launched by the counter-revolution, we come to the logical continuation that in that sense the province should de facto and legally be transformed into a republic. So this is the first but not insignificant steps towards breaking up the territorial integrity of Serbia and Yugoslavia. And, Comrades, we have begun to tackle that. We have come to grips with that both in Kosovo and in Serbia and in Yugoslavia. Among all progressive people. "Bearing in mind all the achievements so far, everything that remains to be done, and much more remains to be done than has been achieved already, we are facing not tasks and obligations but a great party offensive, the goal of which should be the material and cultural development of Kosovo and a free life of dignity for each of its inhabitants. However, we must first of all clarify some misunderstandings. The inhabitants -- when we say 'inhabitants,' we mean all the people living in the province of Kosovo and who are not singled out daily on the basis of their nationality or ethnic affiliation, just as we don't call them out as -- on the basis of their sex or marital status. So we cannot speak either of a minority nation or a majority nation in Kosovo. It is the Serbs and Montenegrins. The Serbs and Montenegrins are not national minorities in relation to the Albanians in Kosovo, just as Albanians are not a national minority in Yugoslavia, but they live together on a footing of equality with all our other nations and nationalities within our three socialist republics. The stand for an ethnically pure Kosovo and economically and politically autonomous one is not possible ideologically, politically or ethnically either, and in the long-run, it is not in the interests of the Albanian people themselves. "Nationalism of this kind would exclude it from its environment and would not only slow it down but would put a stop to its development altogether, both in the economic sense and in a general sense, in a spiritual sense. "Enver Hoxha, through his policy, excluded the Albanian people as an underdeveloped society from Europe and thereby deprived them of taking part in the dynamic life of the present-day world, and this portion of the Albanian people, here and now, are aspiring towards Europe and a modern society and they should not be stopped along that path. Nationalism always means isolation from others, closing in upon oneself within one's own framework. It means lagging behind in development, because without progress and cooperation on an all Yugoslav level and broader afield, there can be no progress. Every nation and nationality which isolates itself is behaving irresponsibly towards its own development. That is why it is we communists in the first place who must do everything to eliminate the consequences of a nationalist and separatist behaviour on the part of the counter-revolutionary forces in Kosovo and also elsewhere in the country. "It is our goal here to emerge from this state of hatred, intolerance, and distrust. It is our goal that all the people of Kosovo should live well, should have a good life, and it is with respect to that goal that I wish to tell you first and foremost, Comrades, that it is your duty to remain here, to stay here. This is your country. These are our homes. These are your cultivated fields and gardens, and your memories lie here. "You're not going to leave your country, are you, just because you live hard there or because you have been weighed down by the injustices and humiliation? It has never been typical of the Serbian Montenegrin people to yield before obstacles and to become demoralised when facing a problem. "As I was saying, to become demoralised when facing a problem, when coming upon hard times. You must stay here because of your ancestors and because of your descendants. Otherwise, your ancestors would be disgraced and your descendants disappointed. "I do not suggest to you, Comrades, that in staying you put up with the suffering and the situation that you're not satisfied with. Quite the contrary. You must change the situation together with all other progressive people here in Serbia and Yugoslavia. Do not say to yourselves that you cannot stand alone. Of course you cannot stand alone, and we shall do it together. We in Serbia and everybody else in Yugoslavia will strive to change the situation. We cannot return the national structure of the Kosovo population, but we can stop further -- the further exodus and provide conditions conducive to a good life to all people in Kosovo, living together and sharing their destiny and the economic opportunities that Kosovo has to offer and every other opportunity. "For some citizens in Europe, this demand seems to be absurd. It seems to be ridiculous to have to voice that demand in the present day world, and they rightly ask themselves about the life and work of the citizens, their security and equality, their rights and duties, because are they not regulated by the constitution and the law? Yes, they are if those laws are applied. When those laws are not applied, then they are not well regulated and that is when all these state authorities and administrative bodies must warn the political platform to do their duty. Their duty to consistently enforce the constitutional laws in Kosovo is a duty that is up to us all; Serbs, Montenegrins, and Albanians as well, Comrades, because if we legalised this state of lawlessness, then all those who are exposed to lawlessness are endangered. "Today it is the Serbs and Montenegrins that suffer most from that, but tomorrow this could be the Albanians, too, and that is why, unless law and order is introduced and respected in the broader social and historical sense, this will be the interest of all of the inhabitants of Kosovo. It is a very urgent matter which we must see to together in Kosovo. "And the second thing is this: We must talk about the return of people to Kosovo, especially experts, professionals. I firmly believe that you cannot stop the process of exodus until people are allowed and able to return to Kosovo. The return of the Serbs and Montenegrins to Kosovo is a process. It cannot be done by decree. People cannot be forced to go where they do not wish to live but we can launch a political campaign in order to provide material, economic, work and cultural conditions conducive to their return to Kosovo so that people who left Kosovo because of injustice and discontent can return. We must provide apartments for them and jobs for them and generally conditions for this to come about. "By creating all these -- in order to create all these conditions, we must harness the strengths of all progressive people, communists, young people, and all honest and progressive people in Serbia. No price is too high to achieve this. "And in -- we usually say in our political language that we're not in favour of campaigns but in favour of permanent lasting processes. In this case, the situation is urgent. It is alarming. We must launch a campaign, a real campaign to ensure that 50, 100, 200 professors, doctors, experts, professionals, skilled workers come back and then others will follow. This campaign must then become a process. Only then can we have any hopes of stopping the exodus of Serbs and Montenegrins from Kosovo. And the spirit of law and justice and progress must be embodied in the working class of Kosovo, because it has identical interests and least interest in becoming divided on a national basis. It is the working class that have always fought successfully against greater injustices. We cannot place our trust in any other people, ladies and gentlemen, Comrades, but in us ourselves. "That is what I wanted to tell you on this occasion, Comrades, with respect to this discussion of ours here today, and I would also like to convince you that every member of the leadership of the Socialist Republic of Serbia and the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia will always be ready for discussions of this kind and for a permanent presence in our joint activities, the joint endeavours discussed here by us today. Rest assured those are the sentiments which prevail throughout Yugoslavia. The whole of Yugoslavia is with you. We are not -- we are conscious of the fact that this is not a problem of Yugoslavia alone. Yugoslavia cannot exist without Kosovo. Yugoslavia will become disintegrated without Kosovo. Yugoslavia and Serbia will not give up Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, before you put any questions on that, I think we -- we will take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the break, I'm sorry if His Honour Judge Kwon and His Honour Judge Bonomy must wonder what I was doing trying to find a transcript. It was indeed in 5.1 but it hadn't been provided to us. It's often a problem that the files coming to the Court have later translations than the translations that are provided to us when we get the files a little earlier. So I took time simply because they hadn't yet been provided to us, and I'm sorry about that. I've now found them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will rise for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're now to formulate questions for the witness, not to make general comments on the strength of the video which we just saw.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best, Mr. Robinson, but before I continue with my questioning of the witness, I'm afraid you might cut me off at a quarter to two, and I want one thing to have been said, a technical observation. Namely, the next witness, due to health considerations, he is supposed to have surgery soon, would need to testify tomorrow morning, so that he would need to be interposed in the testimony of Mr. Balevic. The next witness has very serious medical reasons for this urgency and I hope you will acknowledge and take this into account. The next witness would start tomorrow and finish within one or one and a half sessions and then Mr. Balevic could continue. I hope that you have already been notified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have been notified, and we are in agreement with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, I will read out to you paragraph 76 of the Kosovo indictment, which relates to those events in April, which we have just seen on the TV footage, to follow up on our questions from before. So paragraph 76 reads -- I don't have to read it all because it has been quoted from before. "In meetings with local Serb leaders and in a speech before a crowd of Serbs -" so that is the speech we've just seen - "Slobodan Milosevic endorsed the Serbian nationalist agenda." Sir, my question is: You as the chairman of that meeting, did you or any of your fellow citizens, in view of everything that had happened, have the impression at any point that there was anything in my speech directed against the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you not to interrupt me, and I want to round off one answer that I didn't complete. When we addressed that invitation to Mr. Milosevic or somebody in that position but to our great fortune it was Mr. Milosevic who came, that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rally in Kosovo Polje had already been banned by the Provisional Committee of the League of Communists and the Municipal Committee of the League of Communists and the decision had already been made to hold a gathering of the League of Communists with the representation of Serbs and Albanians in a ratio of 3 to 1, 3 Albanians per 1 Serb. And they had already prepared 20 passes for people whom they had selected for that meeting. So that meeting was supposed to be held instead of the rally, with the prevalence of Albanians. Whatever is written in the indictment, and I don't know who wrote it and I don't know what they were guided by writing something like this, but your speech and my own speech, which this indictment calls nationalist, those allegations have nothing to do with the truth. All the contributions at that rally were permeated by the idea that we can live together with Albanians, that whatever we were saying was not directed against Albanians as such but against extremists and nationalists. Anybody could have written in the indictment that you could have come to Kosovo without anybody's invitation. So the allegation about your endorsement of nationalist agenda is absolutely pointless, groundless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, during this rally or meeting, you followed all the contributions, everything that was said. Was it the leitmotif that the position of Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo was tragic? What was the focus of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... about it coming up and no objection to being questioned about the film, but something that starts off in that way looks like a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is leading, Mr. Milosevic. I think you have to ask a question about what was the essence of the position of Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo, but you cannot ask a question in which you virtually tell the witness the answer. We have been through this before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The essence of that meeting was the drama of the Serbian and Montenegrin peoples in Kosovo and Metohija whose survival was made impossible, and that is why we demanded that you come and talk to us, because Serbs and Montenegrins from Kosovo and Metohija had knocked on every door in the federation, went to see all the leaders but were not met with any understanding, did not receive any promises that they would be protected and defended, and that's why this meeting took place, the meeting to which we had invited you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned in my speech one campaign, albeit a modest campaign because I say let us have 100 or 200 professors or doctors come back. By the standards of that time, by the standards of Serbs and Montenegrins at the time, would it have been a demonstration of support to have 100 or 200 professors, doctors, teachers come back? Looking from the present point of view, it may seem a very modest number, but what was the objective at that time in terms of providing support and expressing solidarity with the people endangered in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: For the Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo and Metohija, even the return of one single Serb, one single family meant a lot. And especially the return of a professional or an expert or a highly skilled person, let alone two or three, because that would have meant something that may have prevented others from fleeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a single speaker who did not speak about the exodus, about the moving out?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: It's a great shame that we couldn't hear all of the 76 speakers that contributed to that meeting. We saw Goran Milic, who was the editor-in-chief of the Croatian television at the time, I recollect. And with the exception of one or two speeches, all contributions spoke about the terror against the Serbs, the need for each people to return, the despair and the wretchedness, because in Serb villages you could hear no more crying or singing because there were no Serbs left. Kosovo remains ethnically pure now. If all the speeches had been shown, the picture would have been much clearer, but I can tell you that with the exception of one or two speeches, everybody spoke about the exodus and about the need to return, and not against Albanians but only against Albanian nationalism and extremism and terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you presided over that meeting and you watched over everybody in that hall, can you remember any officials who were guests at that meeting? I don't think you will be able to recall all of them, but please tell us the names of those you can remember.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I will try. There was the president of the provincial committee, Azem Vllasi, president of the Municipal Committee Radic Halili, there was Kolj Siroka, a member of some sort of leadership at the time, I don't remember his exact position. There was the president of the municipality. I think that was the representation of the Albanian leadership. However, the top leadership of the Provincial Committee was represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We saw at the beginning what the situation was like outside the building when the police intervened. Was order restored very quickly?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. The moment when you addressed people from the window, the order had been restored already, and there were no further incidents. And anyway, the one and only incident had been caused by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did it transpire later that this police intervention had been absolutely unnecessary?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: It was unnecessary, and the situation had been abused in order to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this book Sleepless Nights, on page 334, although there is a number of pages devoted to the report of the Federal Secretariat for the Interior, and I underline not the Republican Serbian Secretariat but the Federal Secretariat of the Interior, on page 320, you even have a photocopy of the document itself where it says that it's a joint working group of the Federal Secretariat of the Interior, addressed to Serbia, and on page 334, I shall quote from only one passage from this report, where it says: "Using rubber truncheons against citizens by employees of the police is not in keeping with provisions of the Articles 100 and 101 of the rules of procedure for conducting the work of law enforcement. According to statements of citizens who have been interviewed by the committee and statements of the policemen, it has been established that coercion measures had been used against 25 citizens. However, based on these statements and reports and other sources of information, one can assume with a great degree of certainty that coercion measures have been used against other citizens as well. However, their number could not be established. It is indubitable -- it is established beyond doubt that coercion measures were used by 14 members of the police force. It can further be assumed that coercion measures were used also by some other policemen, however, their names could not be identified." Another passage reads: "Overall, the total conduct of the citizenry in the mass rally before the cultural hall in Kosovo Polje cannot be assessed as negative or extremist. There was no significant violation of law and order." Can you tell us anything further about the reasons for this intervention by the police and why the joint working group of the Federal Secretariat for the Interior assessed it as unjustified?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: When this report was published, it was taboo. It was very confidential, but I was aware of it even then, and I was invited by the Provincial Secretariat in Pristina to give my statement, and when I came there I asked if I was being interviewed as a witness or as a suspect. However, I found out from those present that the intervention by the police was not -- had not been necessary. There was no definitive conclusion who gave the orders. It was said that it was Destan Daci, chief of the police administration, but whether he had received orders from above was not clear. The commission included republican, federal and provincial organs. But before that, I had already learned that rubber truncheons had been used without any necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, you were next to me when we were leaving the cultural hall and when this unrest was happening, and you can see in this TV footage when I said nobody must beat people. What was that a reference to? You were next to me.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I was next to you. That was the answer to the people standing immediately before you. Nobody else could even hear you because it was a huge mass of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But what were they saying to me?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: "We are being beaten, President. The police is beating us."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is that how the event transpired; they told me they were beating us -- they were beating them?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and you said nobody must beat you but nobody else could hear you apart from those few people standing around you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the truth is that you said, "Nobody must beat you," in response to their complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go on. Do you know anything about the following: Were proceedings instituted against any members of the police force to establish if they had overstepped their authority?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing was done apart from what is written in the report, and I don't know if any measures -- if any other measures had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Vukasin Jokanovic was testifying here, Mr. Nice suggested that the entire event had been stage managed and that the citizenry had been provoked by the police so that the police could then intervene. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: That allegation is absolutely incorrect. There was absolutely no reason for the citizens to provoke the police and they did not do anything of the kind. I can say that most emphatically. All the police had to do was to maintain law and order after the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What was exactly the duration of that meeting in the cultural hall, and how many speakers in total were there?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: It lasted for about 13 hours, and there were about -- there was a total of 76 speakers, 76 live witnesses who testified to the drama of the Serbian and Montenegrin people in Kosovo and Metohija at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Balevic, that on that day, the 25th of April, that meeting was ended in the early hours of the 25th of April, after having lasted all night, are you aware that after I left Kosovo Polje on that day, which is populated mainly by Serbs, I went to another area populated mainly by Albanians where there is a Savnik pipe factory in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, and I heard your speech that you delivered there at the factory Savnik, where most of the staff are Albanians, over 90 per cent, I believe. And I listened to your speech on the radio and on television. And that, again, was a speech of peace, a message of peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. I held a very brief speech there among those Albanians.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's at, gentlemen, tab 3.2, you have an English translation, and I will quote the greatest part of it. It's less than a page long anyway. I will skip the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I am addressing Albanians. Mr. Balevic, is it contested that I was addressing Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: You were, because 90 per cent of the staff in that pipe factory were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was published in my book in 1989. "Over these past years, things have been happening here which have not occurred in civilised countries of the world for centuries. Women and children are being raped, people are being humiliated, physically mistreated."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, the tab number is 5.2. Yes, proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "... Serbs and Montenegrins, are unable to fight against such disgraceful acts. Irrespective of the type and degree of support which the Republic and Federal leaderships may provide, the position of the Serbian and Montenegrin people in Kosovo must be changed by the Albanians in Kosovo to a large degree. 'Progressive, honest people, young people, and above all, understandably, Albanian communists, must be the first, the most decisive and successful fighters against their own nationalism. "This applies not only to the Albanian people; but also to the Serbian and Montenegrin peoples as well as to all other nations in the world. "It is rightful and moral that the most progressive members themselves among each nation be the first to fight against their own nationalism - against all those ugly and inhuman acts, which insult and humiliate other nations. Such ugly and inhuman acts also insult and humiliate the very people whose members committed them. "Albanian citizens must protect not only Serbs and Montenegrins from the disgrace caused by their nationalists but themselves as well. "With each and every rape of a Serbian child, all Albanians are stained if they do not stop such disgraceful acts. "The security of Serbian and Montenegrin children here in Kosovo should be the worry of the Albanian mothers and fathers, and police to a lesser extent. For when the police and army start taking things into their hands, freedom ceases for the guilty and the innocent alike. "Defend justice and preserve the voice of those who can do so." Do you know what was the reaction of the Albanian leadership and Albanians in general to what I said then at the time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't really follow the comments because I had many other problems myself, so I really didn't follow their reaction to this. But I also didn't read anywhere that there was a negative reaction to this speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I should tell you that today I'm stopping at 1.44, 16 minutes to two. Yesterday, as a result of overstaying by five minutes, the afternoon trial started ten to 15 minutes late, and I don't want to develop that kind of reputation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. I understand that fully. I will try to limit myself to the time available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, as in those weeks and in those months you had contacts with many people throughout Yugoslavia, do you know whether the drama of the Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo was a topic that was quite present, widely publicised in the Yugoslavia society?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but nobody reacted to that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since in the parlance used at the time, which can be seen -- which can be seen based on all the speeches and discussions and so on, the term used frequently was "counter-revolution." So was this the qualification given by the Presidency of the SFRY which just had one Serb member?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't claim with any certainty regarding that qualification. However, as far as I remember, it was said that there was a counter-revolution going on in Kosovo and Metohija at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the parlance of the time, was that the gravest qualification that Yugoslav leadership could give?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it clear, then, that the Yugoslav political leadership was aware of the tragical position of the Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yugoslav political leadership was fully aware of that. They received information through all of their channels. And in addition to that, they also heard what the delegations and various representatives of the people informed them about. Therefore, they knew fully well what was going on in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, now please tell me whether, after my visits to Kosovo Polje in April, the 24th and the 25th of April, the Serbs received any kind of advantageous -- did they have any kind of an advantageous position in relation to Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely. They were fully equal to Albanians. They had no special rights over and above what the Albanians had. A municipality was established after your visit. The president of the municipality was an Albanian. President of the trade union was an Albanian. The secretary of the party was also an Albanian. This shows that in the personnel policy there was no discrimination against the Albanians. All nations had equal rights, and the Serbs asked for nothing else. They simply wanted to have equal rights with Albanians in order to ensure the survival of Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether at the time when this drama was unfolding and when the Yugoslav leadership qualified in gravest terms what was going on in Kosovo and Metohija who were the members of the Yugoslav leadership?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the president of the Presidency was Sinan Hasani, who on one occasion as the president of Presidency visited a Serbian village called Prelluzhe just to talk to the residents. He was president of the Presidency, and then Fadil Hodza was also one of the top leaders. If I remember, Kadijevic was also up there. But Sinan Hasani was the president of the Presidency, which is the supreme body in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please explain who Sinan Hasani is.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Sinan Hasani is an Albanian from a village near Gnjilane. So there was an Albanian in the highest post in the country; president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was Sinan Hasani in that office when the amendments to the constitution were passed in 1989?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you just believe that he was? Because if you're not sure, you better not claim this with certainty. It is easy to verify this, at any rate. Now I'm going to put a question to you which pertains directly to you. We had a JNA officer testify here. He was a member of the intelligence service, and he claimed that you conveyed to your daughter-in-law, Ljiljana Balevic, my words to the effect that Romanians would be moved and relegated to Kosovo and Metohija. What can you say concerning that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I've been following this trial. I don't remember the name of that Muslim officer - I'm not interested in his name at all - but this is a flagrant lie. It is such a blatant lie that there is no word in the Serbian vocabulary to describe this. I have never said anything similar to my daughter-in-law. She had no contact with that person whatsoever. It would be similar to a statement to the effect that we are going to relocate and settle Albanians in Bulgaria, someplace like that, because we could not even bring back Serbs who had left Kosovo and gone to live in Nis. So what this gentleman was saying is completely outrageous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, I don't know whether you were at the head or you were just a member of the body which took care of the refugees coming in from Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was the president of the city staff in charge of welcoming the refugees arriving from Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You probably heard that it was stated here that the authorities in Serbia, led by me, wanted to change the national composition of Kosovo and Metohija by populating it with refugees from Croatia and Bosnia. What can you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: As the president of the city staff, I used to greet refugees arriving in Kosovo Polje railway station. Therefore, I know very well the figures of refugees. I think that the figure is between 2 and 3.000. A lot of them later went abroad. So this is a pure fabrication, an unprecedented lie which cannot be corroborated at all. Nobody knows this better than Bane Ivkovic who was the president of the republican staff for refugees. We took in refugees, and as far as Bane told me, it was your position as well, but only those refugees who wished and wanted to come there. These people arrived from the Republic of Serbia and were told by their authorities that they shouldn't go to Kosovo unless they really want to because there is terror there. Therefore, this statement is a pure fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us stick to the facts. You told us that you were the president of the staff welcoming refugees in Pristina, so you know the facts very well. Now, please listen to me carefully. In Kosovo and Metohija, in percentages, were there more refugees from Bosnia and Croatia than other parts of Serbia or not?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I don't know how many refugees there were in Serbia, but we had 3 to 4.000 of refugees, no more than that. And there were around 100.000 refugees in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before going forward, can I clarify this. One witness -- it is about -- you said it is his daughter-in-law, but if my memory is correct, the witness who was referred to by you as that -- it was your sister-in-law, Ljilja Balevic, who had told you -- who had told him something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, in Serbian language, the word "snaha" can refer both to your brother's wife and to your son's wife.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this witness can refer to this person as my mother or as my sister, but in fact this person is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: Either daughter-in-law or sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that can be established, verified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, I don't know if my words were translated to you, but the same term is used both for the brother's wife and the son's wife in Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's clear, yes. I understand. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, in view of your entire experience, and you actively participated in the social and political life of Kosovo and Metohija for several decades, therefore, please tell me, throughout that period of time, was it reasonable, were there any grounds for Albanians to complain about the personnel policy in Kosovo and Metohija or any other injustice done to them?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I've already said several times this was absolutely groundless for them to complain about personnel policy or any other kind of policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, I'm not going to quote any documents that were presented here, but can you tell us about this claim that the Albanians were expelled from their jobs, dismissed, that they were prevented from finding employment in Kosovo and Metohija after 1989?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: In late 1980s, another phenomenon emerged. Many of them, many Albanians left their jobs en masse in order to depict that they were allegedly disenfranchised and persecuted by Serbian officials. There were even Albanians who requested that they be issued a decision dismissing them from their jobs so that they could wave it in the faces of officials. I can claim this with certainty. There might have been some exceptions, but I can claim with certainty that the official policy was as I described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So what is it that prompted Albanians to protest? What made them do that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I told you what institutions they held, what national ethnic key policy was applied, what rights they had. All they wanted was for Kosovo to become a republic. They wanted to secede from Serbia and be annexed to Albania. This is the essence of what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Among the Albanian officials in Kosovo and Metohija, Rrahman Morina was especially prominent and you knew him. Please tell us, what was his position in relation to the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija? Tell us something about him and about his views.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC
utterances.text: Rrahman Morina is an Albanian originally from a village some five to six kilometres from Pec, married to a Serb woman. He's one of the Albanians who had a pro-Yugoslav orientation, but however, he was under sever pressure. He was pressured by his compatriots and he was committed to putting an end to this terror against Serbs, to ensuring conditions for the return of everyone and to ensuring equal rights for everyone. Therefore, he was between the rock and the hard place. On one side pressured by his compatriots; on the other side pressured by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as I indicated, we have to adjourn. Mr. Balevic, your evidence is not concluded. You will return -- you will return tomorrow because your evidence may be completed tomorrow. We are adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just for his own arrangements, his evidence in chief may be completed tomorrow. He is inevitably now going to go into next week. If this witness -- if the other witness is interposed to take one or two sessions, that's inevitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You should appreciate that you may have to be here next week for cross-examination. I imagine Mr. Milosevic and his associates will have explained that to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nobody explained that to me. This is the first time that I heard about this, but that's fine. I will stay as long as you want me to stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You will be required to stay. We are adjourned until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of January, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
